## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

## remarkable
# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

# Atomization brief (shared by every Flint ingest agent)

Read this whole file before writing anything. It holds the rules the Harries review taught (2026-09-26: 25 of 35 files needed fixes). The review gate will check every rule here.

## Schema

Follow `C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\skills\ingest-book\SKILL.md` exactly: `_domain.md`, `_book.md` (map and resume checkpoint, updated after EACH chapter or unit), and entries named `<kind>--<kebab-slug>.md` with kind one of principle, framework, case-study, heuristic, claim. Use the frontmatter keys exactly as the skill gives them. The body has **What it is** / **Why it works** / **When to apply** / **When NOT to apply** (mandatory, non-trivial) / **Example** / **Related**.

Style reference, read before writing: `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library\strength-and-conditioning\fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer\case-study--isometric-sprinter-and-hurdler.md`, plus one principle file in the same folder.

## Voices: label every one

- **The source author's statements are plain text.**
- **Eric's views** (from `docs/method-baseline.md` or his reviews) are prefixed "Eric's baseline:" or "Eric's review:".
- **Your own reasoning, application or synthesis** is prefixed "Inference:".
- **Nothing unlabeled that the author did not say.** The most common failures: a judgment from Eric's review written as if the author said it; a mechanism the author never gave presented as "why it works" (write "The author gives no mechanism. Inference: ..."); an invented example.

## Lessons from the Supertraining Chapter 1 review (2026-09-26: 30 FIX, 1 NO-GO of 41)

- **Keep the source's internal contradictions.** When a book says X on one page and not-X on another, record both with their pages and set `contested`. Never pick one side silently. The NO-GO entry reversed the book's SJ-CMJ strength-deficit rule because the book states it both ways.
- **Name the right voice.** In co-authored books, write "the authors" unless a passage clearly belongs to one author. A passage that names Verkhoshansky in the third person is Siff writing.
- **Keep `proven` rare and scoped.** Scope it to the replicated core (for example, "Hill's force-velocity curve"), never the whole entry, and mark any disputed sentence inside it. Four of eight `proven` ratings were lowered.
- **No mechanism the source does not give.** About a dozen "Why it works" sections supplied physiology the book never states. Label it "Inference:" or leave it out.
- **Do not add "well established" or "modern research shows" without a citation.** Name the paper, or delete the phrase.

## Evidence

- Every number, definition and quote carries a checkable locator: PDF page (and printed page if it differs), or file plus timestamp. Never write "confirmed in PDF" unless you opened that page.
- Never invent a number. Keep ambiguity visible: mark unclear audio or OCR as unclear, and do not harmonize two conflicting numbers from the source; record both with their locators.
- OCR sources (`staging/ocr/*.md`): pages listed as low_confidence in the header must be checked against the page image before any number from them is cited. Use the Read tool on the PDF page, or render it.

## Confidence

- Practitioner courses and lectures: ceiling `supported`.
- Books: `proven` only for established, widely replicated physiology or mechanics. Soviet-era or single-lab empirical findings and training prescriptions: `supported` at most. `untested` for single cases and anecdotes. `contested` where another library source or modern evidence disagrees (say which).

## Dedup and converge

Before each entry, grep `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library` and the staging library (`C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\staging\library`) for the concept. If it is covered, add a new entry only for a genuinely new angle, and link the existing one in Related. List reciprocal-link suggestions in your final report. Never edit files in the vault or another agent's staging folder.

## Baylor context

Read `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\docs\method-baseline.md` (approved). Use it in When to apply, labelled "Eric's baseline:". Department names: Athletic Performance, Athletic Medicine, Applied Performance. Plain style, no em dashes. Use commas, colons and parentheses.

- Write ONLY into your assigned staging folder. No git, no vault edits.
- Stop at a chapter or unit boundary. It is better to finish fewer chapters well; the `_book.md` checkpoint lets the next batch resume.

You are an independent reviewer in Flint's ingest review gate. Another model wrote these entries; your job is to FALSIFY them, not confirm. Read-only on entries and sources. Write only your report file.

# Review: Supertraining Chapter 1 (41 entries + `_book.md`)

Reviewer: Claude Opus (independent falsification pass), 2026-09-26.
Brief: `staging/review_book_prompt.md`. Standards: `docs/ATOMIZE_BRIEF.md`.
Scope: `staging/library/strength-and-conditioning/supertraining--verkhoshansky/*.md`.
Source: `staging/books/supertraining-6th-expanded.pdf`, printed pp. 1-94.

## How the source was checked

- Every entry was compared with the full Chapter 1 text (extracted `st_full.json`, idx 12-104, read in full) and the tables and figures were checked on the page image: Table 1.1 (viewer p. 23), Table 1.2 (viewer p. 37), Table 1.4 (viewer p. 93), the strength-deficit paragraphs (viewer pp. 21-22), Greene & McMahon and the 15-120 ms passage (viewer p. 59), Figs 1.27-1.29 (viewer pp. 75-76), and the chapter opening (viewer p. 13).
- **Locator convention.** The entries' "PDF p. N" is the extractor's 0-based index: printed + 11. A normal 1-based PDF viewer (and the Read tool) shows printed page 1 on page 13, so viewer page = printed + 12. Below, "PDF" means the entries' index (printed + 11), to match the entries. The fix is a single note in `_book.md` (row 1), not 41 separate edits.
- Rule 4 (When NOT present and substantive) was checked for all 41 entries. All have one. The one that is not really a when-not is `principle--rate-of-force-development` (a "developed later" cross-reference plus an inference); see its row.
- Eric's-baseline claims were checked against `docs/method-baseline.md`. Duplicates were checked by grep against `SecondBrain/Knowledge/library` and the staging library.

## Global findings (apply to many rows)

1. **Unlabeled "Why it works" mechanisms.** About a dozen entries give a mechanism the book does not state, with no label. ATOMIZE_BRIEF rule: write "The author gives no mechanism. Inference: ...". Each case is listed in its row.
2. **Author voice.** Many entries write "Verkhoshansky states/argues" for passages that refer to Verkhoshansky in the third person ("developed ... by Verkhoshansky", printed 34; "Verkhoshansky has shown", printed 10; "(Siff, 1998)", printed 35). These passages are in Siff's voice. Correction: write "the authors" or "Verkhoshansky & Siff" unless the text itself names who is speaking.
3. **Harmonized source conflicts.** In five places the book contradicts itself and the entry quietly picks one side: the strength-deficit direction, CAR (superficial vs deep), glycogen-only supercompensation, SEC energy storage by fibre type, and the Table 1.1 "6-80" misprint. ATOMIZE_BRIEF says to record both.

## Entry table

| File | Verdict | Problem (entry vs source, with page) | Exact correction |
|---|---|---|---|
| `_book.md` | FIX | (a) Offset convention not stated. "PDF idx" = printed + 11 is 0-based; in a 1-based viewer, printed 1 = viewer p. 13 (checked with the Read tool: viewer p. 12 is TOC page "x"). ---

# Estimating Strength Deficit by Comparing a Static-Start Jump to a Dip/Countermovement Jump

**What it is** — Strength deficit is defined as the gap between an athlete's maximum
voluntary strength in a given action and their absolute strength (Fmm), the involuntary
ceiling for that same action (see [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]]), "the
difference between maximum strength (voluntary effort) produced in a given action and
absolute strength (involuntary effort) of which the athlete is capable in that same
action" (printed 9). True Fmm requires electrical stimulation, which is impractical and
risky to test directly. As a field proxy, the text proposes comparing a vertical jump from
a static, knees-flexed start (no countermovement) against a vertical jump preceded by a
sudden dip (printed 9).

The book gives two different, conflicting rules for what a small versus large gap means,
and this entry previously took only one side. The jump paragraph itself states: "If there
is a small difference between the two jumps, this suggests that training focuses more on
nervous stimulation via the use of 'shock' and ballistic methods such as plyometrics. If
the deficit is large, then strength and hypertrophy training with 5RM to 8RM ... loads
using methods such as CAT (Compensatory Activation Training) is more suitable" (printed
9-10). The very next paragraph states the opposite pairing as a general rule: "In general,
if the strength deficit is large for a given muscle group, an increase in speed-strength
may be produced by maximal or near-maximal neuromuscular stimulation (e.g. via
weightlifting or plyometric methods). If the strength deficit is small, hypertrophy must be
induced by submaximal loading methods" (printed 10). These two statements directly
conflict on the jump test's own page: a small jump-test gap means shock/ballistic work by
the first statement and hypertrophy-then-heavy-loads by the second; a large gap means
5-8RM CAT strength/hypertrophy work by the first statement and weightlifting/plyometric
work by the second. No direction can be safely taken from this source alone. (PDF pp.
20-21, printed pp. 9-10; the explosive-strength-deficit formalism, Fmax vs. Fmm, is
credited to Zatsiorsky, 1995, discussed further via the force-time curve in Ch3.)

The vault's summary of Kozinc et al. (2022) similarly concludes that a larger CMJ-SJ
difference "is not necessarily better" and "does not validate a diagnostic cutoff or a
training algorithm" (`kozinc-2022-the-difference-between-squat-jump-and-countermovement-jump-in-770-male-and-female-particip`),
which independently argues against using either of this book's two directions as a
programming rule.

**Why it works** — Inference: a countermovement recruits the stretch-shortening cycle and
a degree of involuntary reflex potentiation that a static start cannot access, which is
presumably why the book treats the gap as informative at all; but because the book gives
opposite readings of what a large or small gap implies, no mechanism can be assigned with
confidence to either direction.

**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** the standard CMJ family run on ForceDecks
includes the squat jump (quarter-squat start, static, 3s hold) and the countermovement
jump (x3), among other variants (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular
monitoring," citing `revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md`); mRSI from daily CMJ testing is
the department's chosen daily readiness marker (same section, citing
`2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`). Inference: SJ-vs-CMJ comparison on ForceDecks is a
modern, instrumented analogue of this book's proposed proxy, but given the book's internal
conflict and Kozinc et al. (2022)'s finding that the difference does not validate a
training algorithm, this entry gives no basis for deriving a training-emphasis rule from
that comparison.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not use this framework to set training emphasis from an
SJ/CMJ-style gap in either direction; the book contradicts itself on which direction is
which (printed 9-10), and the modern evidence on this specific test (Kozinc et al. 2022)
does not support a diagnostic cutoff or algorithm built on it. Use RSI, mRSI, or other
modern jump-testing metrics on their own validated basis instead of this 1990s-era
heuristic.

**Example** — Inference: no training-emphasis direction can be taken from this source; see
Kozinc et al. (2022) for the modern evidence on SJ-CMJ differences.

**Related** — [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]],
[[research-papers/kozinc-2022-the-difference-between-squat-jump-and-countermovement-jump-in-770-male-and-female-particip]].

# Strength Deficit Size Points to a Different Training Method

**What it is** — If an athlete's strength deficit (see
[[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]]) is large for a given muscle
group, the "In general" rule on printed 10 recommends near-maximal neuromuscular
stimulation (weightlifting or plyometric methods). If the deficit is small, it recommends
submaximal hypertrophy work (bodybuilding-style loading) followed by maximal efforts
against heavy loads. Note: the jump paragraph on the same page gives the opposite pairing
for the jump-test version of the deficit (large jump-test difference means 5-8RM
strength/hypertrophy work with CAT; small difference means shock/ballistic methods); the
source is internally inconsistent on this point (see
[[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]] for both statements with pages).
The book expands CAT two ways: "Compensatory Activation Training" with 5-8RM loads
(printed 10) and, in the separate CAT technique discussion, "Compensatory Acceleration
Training" for voluntarily managing bar speed, where "Compensatory Action Training" is also
proposed as a broader name (printed 21). The book does not say whether these are the same
method. The authors' own research is cited as finding the strength deficit increases as
external resistance and movement time decrease, meaning it matters most for fast,
low-resistance actions such as running, jumping, and throwing, and matters less for slow,
high-resistance actions. (PDF p. 21, printed p. 10.)

**Why it works** — Inference: a large deficit means there is untapped voluntary/neural
capacity still available, so training that improves recruitment and rate of activation (max
effort or reactive/plyometric methods) has the most room to produce gains. A small deficit
means the athlete is already recruiting close to their ceiling voluntarily, so further
gains require growing the tissue itself (hypertrophy) before neural methods can express
more force. This reasoning applies only to the "In general" rule; the source's own
jump-paragraph rule reverses it (see above).

**When to apply** — **Inference:** as a screening question for method selection, applied
only to a directly-measured strength deficit (not a jump-test proxy, see below): a large
deficit points toward near-maximal/reactive methods (weightlifting, plyometrics) over added
hypertrophy volume, and a small deficit toward a hypertrophy or general-strength emphasis
first, per the "In general" rule (printed 10). This specific application is not stated in
the text.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not treat "CAT" as a single validated modern method name; the
book itself uses it for two different things (5-8RM strength/hypertrophy loading on printed
10, bar-acceleration cueing on printed 21). **Inference:** do not use this rule, in either
direction, to set training emphasis from a jump-test deficit; because the book gives
opposite pairings for the jump-test case specifically (see
[[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]]), and the modern evidence on that
test (Kozinc et al. 2022) does not support a diagnostic cutoff or training algorithm, no
safe programming rule can be derived from the jump-test version of this heuristic. The
"In general" rule quoted above is the more textually supported reading for a directly
measured (non-jump-test) deficit, but even that rests on practitioner experience rather
than controlled data.

**Example** — This entry's earlier example paired a large SJ-CMJ gap with plyometric work,
which is the reversed jump-paragraph reading; it is deleted rather than corrected, since no
direction can be safely drawn from the jump-test version of the deficit. See
[[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]] and Kozinc et al. (2022).

**Related** — [[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]],
[[principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter]],
[[research-papers/kozinc-2022-the-difference-between-squat-jump-and-countermovement-jump-in-770-male-and-female-particip]].

# "Adaptive Reconstruction" vs. "Supercompensation": Verkhoshansky/Siff's Sharper Critique

**What it is** — The authors argue "adaptive reconstruction" is a more accurate term than
"supercompensation" for the body's response to training load. One reason is stated
directly alongside the term: enhanced performance "is not simply the result of increased
stores of bioenergetic substances, but also of structural changes in muscle and other
tissues, as well as enhanced efficiency and rates of bioenergetic and neuromuscular
processing" (printed 84). A second reason comes not from that passage but from the
separate single-factor-model critique in 1.16.3: ATP "has never been shown to deplete
significantly, even after very strenuous exercise," and "no supercompensation has yet been
observed to occur among any of the other biochemicals" besides glycogen; each substance
returns to its initial level on its own timeline, so "the timing of subsequent loads to
stimulate the appropriate type of supercompensation remains indeterminate" (printed 87-88).

The book gives two different definitions of "Current Adaptation Reserves" (CAR) for
opposite ends of the same distinction: printed 83 states "In Russian texts, the former
[i.e. the readily-available, superficial] energy source is referred to as the Current
Adaptation Reserves (CAR)," while the Fig 1.39 caption on printed 84 states "The Deep
Adaptation Energy is often referred to as the Current Adaptation Reserves (CAR) by Russian
authors." Both are recorded here rather than harmonized.

The book also conflicts with itself on supercompensation: printed 85 (citing Platonov,
1988) states "supercompensation of some of the energy sources takes place," while printed
88 states "No supercompensation has yet been observed to occur among any of the other
biochemicals." (PDF pp. 94-99, printed pp. 83-88.)

**Why it works** — Inference: if supercompensation literally meant every adaptation-relevant
substance or structure overshoots baseline on a predictable clock, timing the next training
stimulus to "catch the peak" would be a precise science; the book's own admission that this
overshoot pattern is not established for biochemicals besides glycogen undercuts that
precision and supports treating "the next stimulus should land on a rebound" as a general
heuristic, not a substance-by-substance timing rule.

**When to apply** — This library already carries the supercompensation model in
[[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle]], which itself notes
"contemporary sport science largely prefers the fitness-fatigue (two-factor) model over
literal supercompensation" and recommends treating supercompensation "as a useful mental
model, not a measured prescription." **Inference:** this entry adds the specific mechanism
for that caution (structural/efficiency changes beyond energy stores, and the
glycogen-only overshoot finding) and the CAR terminology, which the Bompa entry does not
include; use both together rather than duplicating either.

**When NOT to apply** — This entry is rated `contested` because it is itself a critique of
a still widely-taught model (supercompensation), argued from a mix of established fact
(structural adaptation beyond energy stores) and an absence-of-evidence claim (no
overshoot observed for other biochemicals) that could be revised by newer measurement
techniques. **Inference:** don't treat "adaptive reconstruction" as a rejection of
periodization practice built on supercompensation timing; the text itself notes
supercompensation theory, despite its shortcomings, had a profound and still-useful impact
on periodization design.

**Example** — **Inference:** glycogen loading before an endurance event is a legitimate
application of true supercompensation; assuming a similarly precise "peak window" exists
for, say, connective tissue remodeling or neuromuscular efficiency gains is not supported
by the same evidence.

**Related** — [[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle]] (reciprocal link
recommended there: note that Supertraining Ch1.16 sharpens the "useful mental model, not a
measured prescription" caution with the specific glycogen-only-overshoot finding and the
CAR/adaptive-reconstruction terminology).

# The Bilateral Deficit: Two Limbs Together Produce Less Force Than the Sum of Each Alone

**What it is** — Force produced during a bilateral (two-limb, e.g. barbell) contraction is
usually less than the sum of the forces each limb produces individually (e.g. dumbbells),
a phenomenon called the bilateral deficit, accompanied by reduced integrated EMG
suggesting the prime movers are less activated bilaterally (Coyle et al. 1981;
Vandervoort et al. 1984). The deficit is reported as insignificant in athletes who always
use their limbs simultaneously in their sport (e.g. weightlifters), and the text
recommends athletes whose sport involves bilateral action of the same muscle groups train
bilaterally to minimize the deficit (Secher, 1975). (PDF p. 39, printed p. 28.)

# Muscle Adapts in Days; Tendon, Ligament, and Bone Take Weeks to Months

**What it is** — Muscle tissue adapts to increased loading within several days, whereas
connective tissues (tendon, ligament, joint capsule) and tissue systems with a high
connective-tissue content (bone, cartilage) only show significant adaptation and
hypertrophy after several weeks to months of progressive loading (McDonagh & Davies,
1984). The authors state training prescription must account for the different
adaptation rates of all involved systems and avoid overtraining whichever system adapts
slowest; they recommend gradual load increases and avoiding impulsive/explosive methods
particularly during General Physical Preparation (GPP) and for relative novices to
strength training. (PDF p. 46, printed p. 35.)

**Why it works** — The author gives no mechanism beyond the differing rates. Inference:
collagen turnover and remodeling are slower than muscle protein synthesis and neural
adaptation, so a program that progresses load at the muscle's adaptation rate can outpace
what tendon, ligament, and bone can structurally tolerate.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** directly supports conservative, gradual load
progression in GPP/early training blocks and for novice athletes specifically, and argues
against introducing high-impulse plyometric or explosive work before a base period of
progressive loading has given connective tissue time to adapt. This is a mechanistic
rationale for why "the athlete feels ready for more" (muscle-level readiness) is not
sufficient justification for a rapid load jump (tendon/bone-level readiness lags behind).

"several days" vs. "several weeks or months") and no athlete-population-specific data; do
not treat it as a precise dosing table. **Inference:** this is a general injury-risk
mechanism, not a substitute for clinical input from Athletic Medicine on a specific
athlete's tissue status or injury history.

**Example** — **Inference:** a novice athlete whose squat strength (muscle-level) is
progressing quickly should still have their loading ramp paced by a longer timeline
(weeks to months) appropriate to tendon and bone adaptation, not by how fast their 1RM is
climbing.

# Estimating Strength Deficit by Comparing a Static-Start Jump to a Dip/Countermovement Jump

**What it is** — Strength deficit is defined as the gap between an athlete's maximum
voluntary strength in a given action and their absolute strength (Fmm), the involuntary
ceiling for that same action (see [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]]), "the
difference between maximum strength (voluntary effort) produced in a given action and
absolute strength (involuntary effort) of which the athlete is capable in that same
action" (printed 9). True Fmm requires electrical stimulation, which is impractical and
risky to test directly. As a field proxy, the text proposes comparing a vertical jump from
a static, knees-flexed start (no countermovement) against a vertical jump preceded by a
sudden dip (printed 9).

The book gives two different, conflicting rules for what a small versus large gap means,
and this entry previously took only one side. The jump paragraph itself states: "If there
is a small difference between the two jumps, this suggests that training focuses more on
nervous stimulation via the use of 'shock' and ballistic methods such as plyometrics. If
the deficit is large, then strength and hypertrophy training with 5RM to 8RM ... loads
using methods such as CAT (Compensatory Activation Training) is more suitable" (printed
9-10). The very next paragraph states the opposite pairing as a general rule: "In general,
if the strength deficit is large for a given muscle group, an increase in speed-strength
may be produced by maximal or near-maximal neuromuscular stimulation (e.g. via
weightlifting or plyometric methods). If the strength deficit is small, hypertrophy must be
induced by submaximal loading methods" (printed 10). These two statements directly
conflict on the jump test's own page: a small jump-test gap means shock/ballistic work by
the first statement and hypertrophy-then-heavy-loads by the second; a large gap means
5-8RM CAT strength/hypertrophy work by the first statement and weightlifting/plyometric
work by the second. No direction can be safely taken from this source alone. (PDF pp.
20-21, printed pp. 9-10; the explosive-strength-deficit formalism, Fmax vs. Fmm, is
credited to Zatsiorsky, 1995, discussed further via the force-time curve in Ch3.)

The vault's summary of Kozinc et al. (2022) similarly concludes that a larger CMJ-SJ
difference "is not necessarily better" and "does not validate a diagnostic cutoff or a
training algorithm" (`kozinc-2022-the-difference-between-squat-jump-and-countermovement-jump-in-770-male-and-female-particip`),
which independently argues against using either of this book's two directions as a
programming rule.

**Why it works** — Inference: a countermovement recruits the stretch-shortening cycle and
a degree of involuntary reflex potentiation that a static start cannot access, which is
presumably why the book treats the gap as informative at all; but because the book gives
opposite readings of what a large or small gap implies, no mechanism can be assigned with
confidence to either direction.

**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** the standard CMJ family run on ForceDecks
includes the squat jump (quarter-squat start, static, 3s hold) and the countermovement
jump (x3), among other variants (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular
monitoring," citing `revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md`); mRSI from daily CMJ testing is
the department's chosen daily readiness marker (same section, citing
`2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`). Inference: SJ-vs-CMJ comparison on ForceDecks is a
modern, instrumented analogue of this book's proposed proxy, but given the book's internal
conflict and Kozinc et al. (2022)'s finding that the difference does not validate a
training algorithm, this entry gives no basis for deriving a training-emphasis rule from
that comparison.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not use this framework to set training emphasis from an
SJ/CMJ-style gap in either direction; the book contradicts itself on which direction is
which (printed 9-10), and the modern evidence on this specific test (Kozinc et al. 2022)
does not support a diagnostic cutoff or algorithm built on it. Use RSI, mRSI, or other
modern jump-testing metrics on their own validated basis instead of this 1990s-era
heuristic.

**Example** — Inference: no training-emphasis direction can be taken from this source; see
Kozinc et al. (2022) for the modern evidence on SJ-CMJ differences.

# "Adaptive Reconstruction" vs. "Supercompensation": Verkhoshansky/Siff's Sharper Critique

**What it is** — The authors argue "adaptive reconstruction" is a more accurate term than
"supercompensation" for the body's response to training load. One reason is stated
directly alongside the term: enhanced performance "is not simply the result of increased
stores of bioenergetic substances, but also of structural changes in muscle and other
tissues, as well as enhanced efficiency and rates of bioenergetic and neuromuscular
processing" (printed 84). A second reason comes not from that passage but from the
separate single-factor-model critique in 1.16.3: ATP "has never been shown to deplete
significantly, even after very strenuous exercise," and "no supercompensation has yet been
observed to occur among any of the other biochemicals" besides glycogen; each substance
returns to its initial level on its own timeline, so "the timing of subsequent loads to
stimulate the appropriate type of supercompensation remains indeterminate" (printed 87-88).

The book gives two different definitions of "Current Adaptation Reserves" (CAR) for
opposite ends of the same distinction: printed 83 states "In Russian texts, the former
[i.e. the readily-available, superficial] energy source is referred to as the Current
Adaptation Reserves (CAR)," while the Fig 1.39 caption on printed 84 states "The Deep
Adaptation Energy is often referred to as the Current Adaptation Reserves (CAR) by Russian
authors." Both are recorded here rather than harmonized.

The book also conflicts with itself on supercompensation: printed 85 (citing Platonov,
1988) states "supercompensation of some of the energy sources takes place," while printed
88 states "No supercompensation has yet been observed to occur among any of the other
biochemicals." (PDF pp. 94-99, printed pp. 83-88.)

**Why it works** — Inference: if supercompensation literally meant every adaptation-relevant
substance or structure overshoots baseline on a predictable clock, timing the next training
stimulus to "catch the peak" would be a precise science; the book's own admission that this
overshoot pattern is not established for biochemicals besides glycogen undercuts that
precision and supports treating "the next stimulus should land on a rebound" as a general
heuristic, not a substance-by-substance timing rule.

**When to apply** — This library already carries the supercompensation model in
[[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle]], which itself notes
"contemporary sport science largely prefers the fitness-fatigue (two-factor) model over
literal supercompensation" and recommends treating supercompensation "as a useful mental
model, not a measured prescription." **Inference:** this entry adds the specific mechanism
for that caution (structural/efficiency changes beyond energy stores, and the
glycogen-only overshoot finding) and the CAR terminology, which the Bompa entry does not
include; use both together rather than duplicating either.

**When NOT to apply** — This entry is rated `contested` because it is itself a critique of
a still widely-taught model (supercompensation), argued from a mix of established fact
(structural adaptation beyond energy stores) and an absence-of-evidence claim (no
overshoot observed for other biochemicals) that could be revised by newer measurement
techniques. **Inference:** don't treat "adaptive reconstruction" as a rejection of
periodization practice built on supercompensation timing; the text itself notes
supercompensation theory, despite its shortcomings, had a profound and still-useful impact
on periodization design.

**Example** — **Inference:** glycogen loading before an endurance event is a legitimate
application of true supercompensation; assuming a similarly precise "peak window" exists
for, say, connective tissue remodeling or neuromuscular efficiency gains is not supported
by the same evidence.

recommended there: note that Supertraining Ch1.16 sharpens the "useful mental model, not a
measured prescription" caution with the specific glycogen-only-overshoot finding and the
CAR/adaptive-reconstruction terminology).

=================== claim--energy-system-contribution-by-sport-table
# Classic Energy-System Percentage Tables by Sport (Fox & Mathews, 1974) — Football Listed at ~90% Phosphagen

**What it is** — The authors reproduce Fox & Mathews' (1974) classic tables (Table 1.4)
estimating the percentage contribution of the short-term (phosphagen/ATP-CP), intermediate
(non-oxidative glycolytic), and long-term (oxidative/aerobic) energy systems to different
training modes and sports. American football is listed at 90% short-term, 10%
intermediate, 0% long-term — among the most phosphagen-dominant sports in the table,
comparable to golf (95/5/0) and volleyball (90/10/0), and far more phosphagen-dominant
than field hockey or soccer half-backs (60/20/20). The authors themselves caution that
"figures for longer duration events such as the 1500m run have been modified by other
researchers and their accuracy needs to be re-examined," that "the highly determinate
nature of this whole scheme, compiled several decades ago, has been questioned more
recently," and that it should not be used casually because it disguises moment-to-moment
metabolic demand shifts within a single sport (printed 81). (PDF pp. 91-92, printed pp.
80-81.)

**Why it works** — The authors state these figures "reflect the average contributions made
by three concurrently operating metabolic systems ... for an average athlete," which
"disguises the fact ... that the metabolic demands often differ from instant to instant
during every type of activity taking place in each sport" (printed 81). Inference: for
football specifically, actual play consists of short high-intensity bursts (plays)
separated by long rest (huddles, substitutions), so an average figure can obscure the real
repeated-sprint, phosphagen-dominant-per-play structure while also underweighting the role
of aerobic recovery between bursts; the text does not itself apply this reasoning to
football.

**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** the department's stated conditioning priority for
football is alactic and aerobic capacity/power for fall-camp and game demands, with
glycolytic conditioning treated as a "worst case scenario" absorbed incidentally rather
than programmed as a primary target (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy
systems," citing `class-4-2026.md pp.34, 39`); the baseline also states the aerobic
system's main value for speed-power athletes is inter-effort recovery (regenerating ATP
between bouts), not distance capacity (citing `2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md
p.9`). **Inference:** this table's 90/10/0 split for football (near-zero credited to the
long-term/aerobic system) looks, at first read, to be in tension with the baseline's
explicit inclusion of aerobic capacity as a Goal-1 priority for football — but the tension
likely resolves once "aerobic system" is understood functionally: the baseline treats
aerobic fitness as enabling faster ATP/phosphagen regeneration between the very
phosphagen-dominant plays this table describes, not as a source of in-play energy. Read
together, not as contradictory: this table describes what fuels a single play; the
baseline describes what determines how well that fuel regenerates for the next one.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors' own caution applies directly here: **Inference:** do
not use the 90/10/0 football figure as a precise or current number; it is a decades-old
average estimate for the sport as a whole, not a modern, position-specific or play-by-play
breakdown. The text itself states that "the highly determinate nature of this whole scheme,
compiled several decades ago, has been questioned more recently" and that figures for
longer events "have been modified by other researchers" (printed 81). This entry is rated
`contested` beyond that self-flagged caution because modern measurement puts the aerobic
contribution far higher, and earlier in an effort, than these 1970s tables allow for (e.g.
Gastin, 2001, Sports Med 31:725-741).

**Example** — **Inference:** a single football play (a few seconds of maximal effort)
draws almost entirely on the phosphagen system, consistent with the table; but the
athlete's ability to repeat that near-maximal output play after play, series after series,
depends heavily on aerobic capacity for recovery between plays — the quality the baseline
prioritizes.

**Related** — None in this ingest yet; candidate future link to a conditioning synthesis
note once Phase 4 of the Flint project reaches conditioning and energy systems.

=================== claim--fiber-recruitment-not-simply-graded-by-force
# The Classic "Slow-Fibres-First-by-Force-Magnitude" Recruitment Model Fails for Ballistic Movement

**What it is** — The standard recruitment scheme gives two different thresholds for slow-
twitch (ST) predominance: ST fibres "are recruited first for muscle tensions up to about
25%" of maximum (printed 59), while elsewhere the text says "ST fibres appear to
predominate in most graded movements requiring less than approximately 20% of the maximum
force capability" (printed 63); both figures are recorded here rather than picked between.
Bosco (1982, cited PDF pp. 74-75, printed pp. 63-64) shows the graded scheme breaks down
for ballistic motion. Walking at moderate speed produces over 700 N of vertical ground
reaction force yet, by contact time and movement pattern, relies almost entirely on
slow-twitch action; a maximal, high-velocity knee extension against a leg-press plate
produces less force than walking despite being nearly pure fast-twitch action. The
force-velocity curve itself differs by jump type: squat jumps and isokinetic testing
reflect mainly the muscle's contractile component and follow the traditional hyperbolic F-V
curve; a countermovement (dip) jump "shift[s]" that curve "upward" while keeping a broadly
similar shape, whereas a depth jump shows "a completely different trend where the force is
no longer inversely proportional to the velocity of movement" (Fig 1.28, printed 64).
Sprinting, high jump, and long jump coordinates also fall far from the traditional F-V
curve. Bosco specifically cautions that isokinetic training is not advisable for athletes
in predominantly ballistic sports.

**Why it works** — Force magnitude alone does not determine which fibres are recruited or
how force is produced; movement pattern, contact duration, and whether elastic energy
storage/release is involved (SSC-mediated ballistic actions vs. purely contractile,
non-ballistic actions) change both the recruitment pattern and the resulting force-time and
force-velocity relationships.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** reinforces
[[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]]: SJ, CMJ, and depth-jump testing
are not interchangeable measures of the same underlying quality, because they load the
contractile component and the SEC to very different degrees. Also reinforces caution about
isokinetic testing/training for ballistic-sport athletes already raised in
[[claim--velocity-and-contraction-specificity-asymmetric-transfer]].

**When NOT to apply** — This entry is rated `contested` rather than `supported` because
orderly (size-principle) recruitment is reported as preserved in ballistic contractions,
with thresholds lowered rather than abandoned (Desmedt & Godaux 1977, J Physiol 264:673),
and because Bosco's own scheme is based on a few illustrative cases (walking, car-pushing,
seated knee extension) rather than a systematic dataset. **Inference:** treat the classic
graded model as a reasonable first approximation for slow, controlled movement, and this
critique as the more accurate account specifically for ballistic/SSC-involved movement.

**Example** — **Inference:** a coach should not assume a squat-jump-based force
measurement predicts depth-jump or sprint ground-reaction performance; the elastic
contribution present in the latter two is largely absent from the former.

**Related** — [[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]],
[[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]].

=================== claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence
# Biochemical Adaptations Occur in a Fixed Order, and Reverse in the Opposite Order When Training Stops

**What it is** — Citing Platonov (1988), the authors state biochemical adaptation to
training follows a definite three-stage sequence, not a simultaneous shift: first,
oxidative ATP resynthesis potential and glycogen level increase; next, structural muscle
protein (myosin) and the intensity of non-oxidative ATP resynthesis (glycolysis) increase;
only after that does creatine phosphate (CP) level rise. During overtraining specifically,
these adaptations are lost "in an order that is the reverse of the order seen during
training." The longer the training period, the more thorough the adaptation and the longer
those biochemical changes persist after training stops (especially glycogen and CP levels).
This gain/loss asymmetry across different systems is termed heterochronic (different
tissues and processes change on different timelines). Overtraining specifically also shows
a distinct pattern: reduced glycogenolytic activity, decreased ascorbic acid/glutathione/
glycogen, blood plasma dysproteinaemia, and reduced sympathico-adrenal function tied to
disrupted acid-base balance. (PDF pp. 96-97, printed pp. 85-86.)

**Why it works** — Inference: different adaptations (enzymatic/oxidative capacity,
structural protein synthesis, phosphagen system capacity) depend on different cellular
mechanisms with different synthesis and degradation rates, so a uniform "the body adapts,
then de-adapts" model misses that some qualities are gained early and lost late, while
others are gained late and lost early. The author gives no such mechanism directly; this is
this entry's own reading of the stated sequence.

**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** the department's own conditioning material states
that traits easiest to build (aerobic) are lost fastest under detraining, while traits
hardest to build (alactic/speed) are lost slowest, and uses this ordering to sequence how
often each quality needs re-exposure (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy
systems," citing `class-4-2026.md p.47`). **Inference:** this converges directionally with
Platonov's heterochronic principle (different systems have different adaptation/de-
adaptation timelines) but the two are not a stated one-to-one match — the baseline's
build-easy/lose-fast claim is about energy-system categories (aerobic vs. alactic), while
Platonov's sequence is about biochemical sub-processes within training generally (oxidative
capacity, structural protein, glycolysis, CP). Treat them as parallel instances of the same
underlying heterochronicity concept, not as the same specific claim restated.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the specific ordering (oxidative/glycogen, then
structural protein/glycolysis, then CP) is cited to one secondary source (Platonov, 1988)
without the underlying primary data described in this text; do not treat this exact
three-stage sequence as a settled, universally-timed protocol for monitoring detraining. Use
it as a general principle (adaptation and loss are not uniform across systems) rather than
a specific testing checklist. The source states the reverse-order loss for overtraining,
not for simple layoffs; the entry's own extension to detraining/layoffs beyond what the
text states is this entry's inference, not the authors' claim.

**Example** — Inference: by the stated reverse order, CP-related qualities (gained last)
would be lost first, and oxidative and glycogen qualities lost last. The source states this
reverse order for overtraining, not for a training layoff; it separately notes that longer
training makes the accompanying biochemical changes persist longer after cessation
(printed 86), which is the closest the text comes to describing simple detraining.

**Related** — [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]].

=================== claim--lactate-and-oxygen-debt-myths
# Lactate Does Not "Poison" Muscle or Cause Soreness; "Oxygen Debt" Is an Outdated Concept

**What it is** — Two corrections to common misconceptions. (1) Muscle fatigue is not due
to "lactic acid poisoning"; lactate formation is accompanied by hydrogen ions that increase
acidity and can interfere with contraction and enzyme efficiency, but lactate itself is not
the toxin popularly described, and blood lactate returns to normal within about an hour of
strenuous interval training — well before delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) typically
peaks. The most pronounced soreness actually occurs after prolonged endurance efforts kept
below the lactate threshold, so current theory attributes soreness to transient muscle
cell or connective tissue damage, not lactic acid. (2) The classic "oxygen debt" concept
(the idea that post-exercise heavy breathing "repays" an oxygen deficit incurred during
anaerobic work) is now considered outdated; the post-exercise period instead reflects
recovery oxygen consumption used to regenerate ATP and CP and restore respiratory, ionic,
circulatory, hormonal, and thermal systems to baseline (McArdle, Katch & Katch, 1991). The
text says the former "anaerobic threshold" is now referred to as the "blood lactate
threshold (or turnpoint) or OBLA (Onset of Blood Lactate Accumulation)" (printed 78). (PDF
pp. 87, 89, printed pp. 76, 78.)

**Why it works** — Both corrections reflect the same underlying update in exercise
physiology: lactate is a normal metabolic byproduct and fuel source, not an anaerobic waste
product to be "cleared" or "repaid," and glycolysis runs alongside oxidative metabolism
rather than only replacing it when oxygen is absent (also noted in this book: glycolysis
dominates during sprinting even though muscles have adequate oxygen).

**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful for correcting persistent coaching-room and
classroom misconceptions (e.g. in HHPR 5355 teaching) — "lactic acid causes the burn and
next-day soreness" and "you're paying back oxygen debt after a sprint" are both outdated
framings that this entry can directly correct with citable sources.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** correcting the mechanism does not mean lactate is
irrelevant to training; the blood lactate threshold (OBLA) remains a legitimate, useful
marker for endurance training intensity and athlete conditioning status — only the
"lactic acid as toxin/soreness cause" framing and the "oxygen debt" framing are being
corrected here, not the practical value of lactate-threshold-based training zones.
Inference: the H+/acidosis fatigue mechanism the authors give here (increased acidity
"can interfere with the muscle contraction process") is itself contested in modern work
(Westerblad, Allen & Lannergren 2002, News Physiol Sci 17:17; Allen, Lamb & Westerblad
2008, Physiol Rev 88:287); `proven` here covers only the two named corrections (lactate is
not the cause of DOMS; oxygen debt is replaced by recovery oxygen consumption and EPOC),
not the H+/acidosis fatigue mechanism.

**Example** — **Inference:** an athlete sore two days after a hard endurance session is
more likely dealing with muscle/connective tissue microtrauma than residual lactate, which
would have cleared within an hour; recovery guidance should be based on that, not on
"flushing out lactic acid."

**Related** — [[claim--energy-system-contribution-by-sport-table]].

=================== claim--strength-training-threshold-stimulus
# A Minimum Load Threshold Drives Strength Gains, and It Rises as the Athlete Adapts

**What it is** — Hettinger & Muller (1953) are cited for a threshold training stimulus of
roughly one-third of maximal strength needed to produce a strength increase in an average
person; as strength rises, the required stimulus intensity rises too, eventually reaching
80-95% of the athlete's maximum, sometimes matching or exceeding actual competition
intensity (Verkhoshansky, 1977). Each stimulus level has its own "strengthening
threshold," a ceiling beyond which no further gain occurs at that intensity, and this
ceiling is described as further from the untrained state the less trained the athlete is.
Separately, Korobkov, Gerasimov & Vasiliev (via Verkhoshansky, 1977) are cited for the
finding that in the initial stages of training, strength increases roughly uniformly
regardless of load, with approximately equivalent gains reported at 20%, 40%, 60% and 80%
of 1RM; raising training intensity early (heavier load, faster tempo, shorter intervals
between sessions) does not reliably improve on this until strength has already progressed
some way. (PDF pp. 33-34, printed pp. 22-23.)

**Why it works** — The author gives no mechanism. Inference: early neuromuscular
adaptation (see
[[principle--neuromuscular-stimulation-drives-early-strength-gains]]) responds to almost
any sufficiently repeated stimulus above a low floor; once that easy adaptive window
closes, further progress requires a stimulus that approaches the athlete's current
ceiling, because there is less slack left in recruitment and coordination to exploit.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** supports keeping early-phase (novice) load prescription
simple and consistency-focused rather than chasing high intensities, and supports
progressively raising relative intensity toward 80-95% of max as an athlete's training age
increases, consistent with this book's own training-age-scaling heuristic
([[heuristic--program-variable-complexity-scales-with-training-age]]).

**When NOT to apply** — These are single-source, decades-old figures cited without a
stated sample or modern replication in this text (Hettinger 1961; Korobkov, Gerasimov &
Vasiliev via Verkhoshansky 1977; PDF pp. 33-34, printed pp. 22-23). **Inference:** do not
treat "one-third of max" or the specific 20/40/60/80% equivalence as precise, universal
cutoffs for a current athlete population; use them as a directional argument for why novice
programming can be simple, not as exact percentages to program from.

**Example** — **Inference:** A true beginner's program built around consistent submaximal loading (e.g.
50-60% 1RM) can produce comparable early strength gains to a heavier protocol, so there is
little value in front-loading high intensity before the athlete has trained long enough to
need it.

**Related** — [[heuristic--program-variable-complexity-scales-with-training-age]],
[[periodization--bompa/principle--progressive-overload-threshold]].

=================== claim--velocity-and-contraction-specificity-asymmetric-transfer
# High-Velocity Training Transfers to Low Velocity Better Than the Reverse; Contraction Modes Barely Cross Over

**What it is** — Two specific, cited findings under the specificity umbrella: (1)
low-velocity isokinetic training improves low-velocity strength but has minimal effect on
high-velocity strength; high-velocity isokinetic training improves high-velocity strength
and transfers somewhat better to low-velocity strength than the reverse direction
(Moffroid & Whipple 1970; Perrine & Edgerton 1981; Kanehisa & Miyashita 1983b). (2)
Contraction-mode adaptations are narrow: concentric-eccentric (weightlifting-style)
training raises competitive strength but produces only small isometric or concentric
isokinetic gains; isometric training raises isometric strength but not concentric
isokinetic strength; elbow-extension training with weights increases triceps strength and
girth without a matching isokinetic-strength change. Static and dynamic training even
produce different microscopic structural changes in the muscle. (PDF pp. 38-40, printed
pp. 27-29.)

**Why it works** — The authors give no reason for the asymmetry itself. What they do say
(printed 29): because force decreases with velocity on the concentric F-V curve, "high
velocity training may not produce a large enough force to stimulate maximal adaptation in
the muscle," but its "special advantage ... is that it conditions the nervous system,
whereas lower velocity training is better suited to development of muscle hypertrophy and
slow speed strength." Inference: force-velocity curve position (see
[[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]]) and contraction-mode
recruitment patterns are trained narrowly because different neural drive strategies and
structural adaptations underlie each.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** when selecting exercise velocity and contraction mode,
match both to the sport action being targeted, and consider biasing toward higher-velocity
work when in doubt, since the text's cited data shows it transfers in both directions
somewhat, whereas slow, heavy work transfers poorly to fast actions. This bias is not
unconditional: the text itself states lower-velocity training is better suited to muscle
hypertrophy and slow-speed strength (printed 29), so the choice should still follow the
target quality, not default to high velocity in every case. **Eric's baseline:**
the isometric seated calf raise and other isometric testing are run on the ForceDecks
"Mid-Thigh Pull" setting as part of the department's standard protocol
(`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing
`protocol-iso-seated-calf-raise.md`, `revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md`). **Inference:**
this claim's contraction-mode specificity finding supports treating isometric testing as
its own distinct quality rather than a proxy for dynamic 1RM strength; neither source states
this connection directly.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** these are 1970s-1980s isokinetic-dynamometer
studies (PDF pp. 38-40, printed pp. 27-29); isokinetic machine training is a narrow,
lab-style modality rarely used in current collegiate S&C practice, and this specific
transfer asymmetry has not been independently re-verified here for free-weight or
plyometric training modes. **Inference:** do not assume the same asymmetric-transfer ratio
applies to, say, barbell velocity-based training without separate evidence; this extension
is not addressed in the text.

**Example** — **Inference:** An athlete tested for isometric mid-thigh pull strength should not be assumed
to have an equivalent dynamic 1RM or sprint force capability; each needs its own
assessment and, if targeted, its own specific training exposure.

**Related** — [[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]].

=================== claim--voluntary-involuntary-strength-reserve-magnitudes
# The Voluntary-Involuntary Strength Reserve Has a Measured Size

**What it is** — Two cited figures quantify how much force voluntary effort leaves
unused relative to the athlete's true ceiling. (1) In experienced weightlifters, the mean
gap between training maximum (TFmax) and competitive maximum (CFmax) is about 12.5 ± 2.5%,
larger in heavier weight classes (Zatsiorsky, 1995; PDF p. 13, printed p. 2). (2) Under
involuntary or hypnotic conditions, strength output can rise by up to 35% in untrained
people, but by less than 10% in trained athletes (PDF p. 13, printed p. 2, no primary
citation given in text for this figure).

**Why it works** — The authors give the protective-governor idea: "specific neural feedback
mechanisms, like governors in a mechanical engine, exist to prevent a muscle from
continuing to produce force to the point of mechanical failure" (printed 1). Inference:
both figures reflect that inhibition; anything that reduces it (competitive arousal,
hypnosis, involuntary reflex recruitment) exposes more of the muscle's true contractile
ceiling. Training may narrow the untapped reserve because part of the strength-training
adaptation is learning to recruit and inhibit less, not just growing tissue; the text does
not state this training mechanism directly.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this is best used as a coaching narrative for why
max-effort numbers move around by context (weigh-in day nerves, meet atmosphere, testing
environment), and as a rough expectation that a smaller gap between training and
competitive/testing efforts is itself a marker of higher training status. Neither the
book nor Eric's baseline states this as an applied rule; it is this entry's own synthesis
of the two cited numbers.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors give no primary citation for the hypnosis figure
(PDF p. 13, printed p. 2); treat it as a single, unverified secondary claim, not a number
to plan around. The 12.5 ± 2.5% figure is stated specifically for experienced Olympic
weightlifters under meet conditions (Zatsiorsky, 1995; PDF p. 13, printed p. 2).
**Inference:** it should not be assumed to transfer directly to Baylor's team-sport
athletes tested on a force plate (ForceDecks CMJ/IMTP) rather than in a weightlifting
competition, and neither number should be used as a correction factor applied to that data
without independent verification; this caution is this entry's own judgment, not stated in
`method-baseline.md`.

**Example** — **Inference:** An athlete who tests near-identically on a submaximal VBT-estimated 1RM and
a rare true max attempt is showing a small reserve gap; a large, inconsistent gap between
estimated and tested max may point to arousal/readiness on test day rather than a change
in underlying capacity.

**Related** — [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]].

no longer inversely proportional to the velocity of movement" (Fig 1.28, printed 64).
Sprinting, high jump, and long jump coordinates also fall far from the traditional F-V
curve. Bosco specifically cautions that isokinetic training is not advisable for athletes
in predominantly ballistic sports.

**Why it works** — Force magnitude alone does not determine which fibres are recruited or
how force is produced; movement pattern, contact duration, and whether elastic energy
storage/release is involved (SSC-mediated ballistic actions vs. purely contractile,
non-ballistic actions) change both the recruitment pattern and the resulting force-time and
force-velocity relationships.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** reinforces
[[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]]: SJ, CMJ, and depth-jump testing
are not interchangeable measures of the same underlying quality, because they load the
contractile component and the SEC to very different degrees. Also reinforces caution about
isokinetic testing/training for ballistic-sport athletes already raised in
[[claim--velocity-and-contraction-specificity-asymmetric-transfer]].

**When NOT to apply** — This entry is rated `contested` rather than `supported` because
orderly (size-principle) recruitment is reported as preserved in ballistic contractions,
with thresholds lowered rather than abandoned (Desmedt & Godaux 1977, J Physiol 264:673),
and because Bosco's own scheme is based on a few illustrative cases (walking, car-pushing,
seated knee extension) rather than a systematic dataset. **Inference:** treat the classic
graded model as a reasonable first approximation for slow, controlled movement, and this
critique as the more accurate account specifically for ballistic/SSC-involved movement.

**Example** — **Inference:** a coach should not assume a squat-jump-based force
measurement predicts depth-jump or sprint ground-reaction performance; the elastic
contribution present in the latter two is largely absent from the former.

**Related** — [[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]],
[[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]].

=================== claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence
# Biochemical Adaptations Occur in a Fixed Order, and Reverse in the Opposite Order When Training Stops

**What it is** — Citing Platonov (1988), the authors state biochemical adaptation to
training follows a definite three-stage sequence, not a simultaneous shift: first,
oxidative ATP resynthesis potential and glycogen level increase; next, structural muscle
protein (myosin) and the intensity of non-oxidative ATP resynthesis (glycolysis) increase;
only after that does creatine phosphate (CP) level rise. During overtraining specifically,
these adaptations are lost "in an order that is the reverse of the order seen during
training." The longer the training period, the more thorough the adaptation and the longer
those biochemical changes persist after training stops (especially glycogen and CP levels).
This gain/loss asymmetry across different systems is termed heterochronic (different
tissues and processes change on different timelines). Overtraining specifically also shows
a distinct pattern: reduced glycogenolytic activity, decreased ascorbic acid/glutathione/
glycogen, blood plasma dysproteinaemia, and reduced sympathico-adrenal function tied to
disrupted acid-base balance. (PDF pp. 96-97, printed pp. 85-86.)

**Why it works** — Inference: different adaptations (enzymatic/oxidative capacity,
structural protein synthesis, phosphagen system capacity) depend on different cellular
mechanisms with different synthesis and degradation rates, so a uniform "the body adapts,
then de-adapts" model misses that some qualities are gained early and lost late, while
others are gained late and lost early. The author gives no such mechanism directly; this is
this entry's own reading of the stated sequence.

**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** the department's own conditioning material states
that traits easiest to build (aerobic) are lost fastest under detraining, while traits
hardest to build (alactic/speed) are lost slowest, and uses this ordering to sequence how
often each quality needs re-exposure (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy
systems," citing `class-4-2026.md p.47`). **Inference:** this converges directionally with
Platonov's heterochronic principle (different systems have different adaptation/de-
adaptation timelines) but the two are not a stated one-to-one match — the baseline's
build-easy/lose-fast claim is about energy-system categories (aerobic vs. alactic), while
Platonov's sequence is about biochemical sub-processes within training generally (oxidative
capacity, structural protein, glycolysis, CP). Treat them as parallel instances of the same
underlying heterochronicity concept, not as the same specific claim restated.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the specific ordering (oxidative/glycogen, then
structural protein/glycolysis, then CP) is cited to one secondary source (Platonov, 1988)
without the underlying primary data described in this text; do not treat this exact
three-stage sequence as a settled, universally-timed protocol for monitoring detraining. Use
it as a general principle (adaptation and loss are not uniform across systems) rather than
a specific testing checklist. The source states the reverse-order loss for overtraining,
not for simple layoffs; the entry's own extension to detraining/layoffs beyond what the
text states is this entry's inference, not the authors' claim.

**Example** — Inference: by the stated reverse order, CP-related qualities (gained last)
would be lost first, and oxidative and glycogen qualities lost last. The source states this
reverse order for overtraining, not for a training layoff; it separately notes that longer
training makes the accompanying biochemical changes persist longer after cessation
(printed 86), which is the closest the text comes to describing simple detraining.

**Related** — [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]].

=================== claim--lactate-and-oxygen-debt-myths
# Lactate Does Not "Poison" Muscle or Cause Soreness; "Oxygen Debt" Is an Outdated Concept

**What it is** — Two corrections to common misconceptions. (1) Muscle fatigue is not due
to "lactic acid poisoning"; lactate formation is accompanied by hydrogen ions that increase
acidity and can interfere with contraction and enzyme efficiency, but lactate itself is not
the toxin popularly described, and blood lactate returns to normal within about an hour of
strenuous interval training — well before delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) typically
peaks. The most pronounced soreness actually occurs after prolonged endurance efforts kept
below the lactate threshold, so current theory attributes soreness to transient muscle
cell or connective tissue damage, not lactic acid. (2) The classic "oxygen debt" concept
(the idea that post-exercise heavy breathing "repays" an oxygen deficit incurred during
anaerobic work) is now considered outdated; the post-exercise period instead reflects
recovery oxygen consumption used to regenerate ATP and CP and restore respiratory, ionic,
circulatory, hormonal, and thermal systems to baseline (McArdle, Katch & Katch, 1991). The
text says the former "anaerobic threshold" is now referred to as the "blood lactate
threshold (or turnpoint) or OBLA (Onset of Blood Lactate Accumulation)" (printed 78). (PDF
pp. 87, 89, printed pp. 76, 78.)

**Why it works** — Both corrections reflect the same underlying update in exercise
physiology: lactate is a normal metabolic byproduct and fuel source, not an anaerobic waste
product to be "cleared" or "repaid," and glycolysis runs alongside oxidative metabolism
rather than only replacing it when oxygen is absent (also noted in this book: glycolysis
dominates during sprinting even though muscles have adequate oxygen).

**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful for correcting persistent coaching-room and
classroom misconceptions (e.g. in HHPR 5355 teaching) — "lactic acid causes the burn and
next-day soreness" and "you're paying back oxygen debt after a sprint" are both outdated
framings that this entry can directly correct with citable sources.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** correcting the mechanism does not mean lactate is
irrelevant to training; the blood lactate threshold (OBLA) remains a legitimate, useful
marker for endurance training intensity and athlete conditioning status — only the
"lactic acid as toxin/soreness cause" framing and the "oxygen debt" framing are being
corrected here, not the practical value of lactate-threshold-based training zones.
Inference: the H+/acidosis fatigue mechanism the authors give here (increased acidity
"can interfere with the muscle contraction process") is itself contested in modern work
(Westerblad, Allen & Lannergren 2002, News Physiol Sci 17:17; Allen, Lamb & Westerblad
2008, Physiol Rev 88:287); `proven` here covers only the two named corrections (lactate is
not the cause of DOMS; oxygen debt is replaced by recovery oxygen consumption and EPOC),
not the H+/acidosis fatigue mechanism.

**Example** — **Inference:** an athlete sore two days after a hard endurance session is
more likely dealing with muscle/connective tissue microtrauma than residual lactate, which
would have cleared within an hour; recovery guidance should be based on that, not on
"flushing out lactic acid."

**Related** — [[claim--energy-system-contribution-by-sport-table]].

=================== claim--strength-training-threshold-stimulus
# A Minimum Load Threshold Drives Strength Gains, and It Rises as the Athlete Adapts

**What it is** — Hettinger & Muller (1953) are cited for a threshold training stimulus of
roughly one-third of maximal strength needed to produce a strength increase in an average
person; as strength rises, the required stimulus intensity rises too, eventually reaching
80-95% of the athlete's maximum, sometimes matching or exceeding actual competition
intensity (Verkhoshansky, 1977). Each stimulus level has its own "strengthening
threshold," a ceiling beyond which no further gain occurs at that intensity, and this
ceiling is described as further from the untrained state the less trained the athlete is.
Separately, Korobkov, Gerasimov & Vasiliev (via Verkhoshansky, 1977) are cited for the
finding that in the initial stages of training, strength increases roughly uniformly
regardless of load, with approximately equivalent gains reported at 20%, 40%, 60% and 80%
of 1RM; raising training intensity early (heavier load, faster tempo, shorter intervals
between sessions) does not reliably improve on this until strength has already progressed
some way. (PDF pp. 33-34, printed pp. 22-23.)

**Why it works** — The author gives no mechanism. Inference: early neuromuscular
adaptation (see
[[principle--neuromuscular-stimulation-drives-early-strength-gains]]) responds to almost
any sufficiently repeated stimulus above a low floor; once that easy adaptive window
closes, further progress requires a stimulus that approaches the athlete's current
ceiling, because there is less slack left in recruitment and coordination to exploit.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** supports keeping early-phase (novice) load prescription
simple and consistency-focused rather than chasing high intensities, and supports
progressively raising relative intensity toward 80-95% of max as an athlete's training age
increases, consistent with this book's own training-age-scaling heuristic
([[heuristic--program-variable-complexity-scales-with-training-age]]).

**When NOT to apply** — These are single-source, decades-old figures cited without a
stated sample or modern replication in this text (Hettinger 1961; Korobkov, Gerasimov &
Vasiliev via Verkhoshansky 1977; PDF pp. 33-34, printed pp. 22-23). **Inference:** do not
treat "one-third of max" or the specific 20/40/60/80% equivalence as precise, universal
cutoffs for a current athlete population; use them as a directional argument for why novice
programming can be simple, not as exact percentages to program from.

**Example** — **Inference:** A true beginner's program built around consistent submaximal loading (e.g.
50-60% 1RM) can produce comparable early strength gains to a heavier protocol, so there is
little value in front-loading high intensity before the athlete has trained long enough to
need it.

**Related** — [[heuristic--program-variable-complexity-scales-with-training-age]],
[[periodization--bompa/principle--progressive-overload-threshold]].

=================== claim--velocity-and-contraction-specificity-asymmetric-transfer
# High-Velocity Training Transfers to Low Velocity Better Than the Reverse; Contraction Modes Barely Cross Over

**What it is** — Two specific, cited findings under the specificity umbrella: (1)
low-velocity isokinetic training improves low-velocity strength but has minimal effect on
high-velocity strength; high-velocity isokinetic training improves high-velocity strength
and transfers somewhat better to low-velocity strength than the reverse direction
(Moffroid & Whipple 1970; Perrine & Edgerton 1981; Kanehisa & Miyashita 1983b). (2)
Contraction-mode adaptations are narrow: concentric-eccentric (weightlifting-style)
training raises competitive strength but produces only small isometric or concentric
isokinetic gains; isometric training raises isometric strength but not concentric
isokinetic strength; elbow-extension training with weights increases triceps strength and
girth without a matching isokinetic-strength change. Static and dynamic training even
produce different microscopic structural changes in the muscle. (PDF pp. 38-40, printed
pp. 27-29.)

**Why it works** — The authors give no reason for the asymmetry itself. What they do say
(printed 29): because force decreases with velocity on the concentric F-V curve, "high
velocity training may not produce a large enough force to stimulate maximal adaptation in
the muscle," but its "special advantage ... is that it conditions the nervous system,
whereas lower velocity training is better suited to development of muscle hypertrophy and
slow speed strength." Inference: force-velocity curve position (see
[[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]]) and contraction-mode
recruitment patterns are trained narrowly because different neural drive strategies and
structural adaptations underlie each.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** when selecting exercise velocity and contraction mode,
match both to the sport action being targeted, and consider biasing toward higher-velocity
work when in doubt, since the text's cited data shows it transfers in both directions
somewhat, whereas slow, heavy work transfers poorly to fast actions. This bias is not
unconditional: the text itself states lower-velocity training is better suited to muscle
hypertrophy and slow-speed strength (printed 29), so the choice should still follow the
target quality, not default to high velocity in every case. **Eric's baseline:**
the isometric seated calf raise and other isometric testing are run on the ForceDecks
"Mid-Thigh Pull" setting as part of the department's standard protocol
(`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing
`protocol-iso-seated-calf-raise.md`, `revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md`). **Inference:**
this claim's contraction-mode specificity finding supports treating isometric testing as
its own distinct quality rather than a proxy for dynamic 1RM strength; neither source states
this connection directly.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** these are 1970s-1980s isokinetic-dynamometer
studies (PDF pp. 38-40, printed pp. 27-29); isokinetic machine training is a narrow,
lab-style modality rarely used in current collegiate S&C practice, and this specific
transfer asymmetry has not been independently re-verified here for free-weight or
plyometric training modes. **Inference:** do not assume the same asymmetric-transfer ratio
applies to, say, barbell velocity-based training without separate evidence; this extension
is not addressed in the text.

**Example** — **Inference:** An athlete tested for isometric mid-thigh pull strength should not be assumed
to have an equivalent dynamic 1RM or sprint force capability; each needs its own
assessment and, if targeted, its own specific training exposure.

**Related** — [[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]].
