=================== claim--voluntary-involuntary-strength-reserve-magnitudes
# The Voluntary-Involuntary Strength Reserve Has a Measured Size

**What it is** — Two cited figures quantify how much force voluntary effort leaves
unused relative to the athlete's true ceiling. (1) In experienced weightlifters, the mean
gap between training maximum (TFmax) and competitive maximum (CFmax) is about 12.5 ± 2.5%,
larger in heavier weight classes (Zatsiorsky, 1995; PDF p. 13, printed p. 2). (2) Under
involuntary or hypnotic conditions, strength output can rise by up to 35% in untrained
people, but by less than 10% in trained athletes (PDF p. 13, printed p. 2, no primary
citation given in text for this figure).

**Why it works** — The authors give the protective-governor idea: "specific neural feedback
mechanisms, like governors in a mechanical engine, exist to prevent a muscle from
continuing to produce force to the point of mechanical failure" (printed 1). Inference:
both figures reflect that inhibition; anything that reduces it (competitive arousal,
hypnosis, involuntary reflex recruitment) exposes more of the muscle's true contractile
ceiling. Training may narrow the untapped reserve because part of the strength-training
adaptation is learning to recruit and inhibit less, not just growing tissue; the text does
not state this training mechanism directly.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this is best used as a coaching narrative for why
max-effort numbers move around by context (weigh-in day nerves, meet atmosphere, testing
environment), and as a rough expectation that a smaller gap between training and
competitive/testing efforts is itself a marker of higher training status. Neither the
book nor Eric's baseline states this as an applied rule; it is this entry's own synthesis
of the two cited numbers.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors give no primary citation for the hypnosis figure
(PDF p. 13, printed p. 2); treat it as a single, unverified secondary claim, not a number
to plan around. The 12.5 ± 2.5% figure is stated specifically for experienced Olympic
weightlifters under meet conditions (Zatsiorsky, 1995; PDF p. 13, printed p. 2).
**Inference:** it should not be assumed to transfer directly to Baylor's team-sport
athletes tested on a force plate (ForceDecks CMJ/IMTP) rather than in a weightlifting
competition, and neither number should be used as a correction factor applied to that data
without independent verification; this caution is this entry's own judgment, not stated in
`method-baseline.md`.

**Example** — **Inference:** An athlete who tests near-identically on a submaximal VBT-estimated 1RM and
a rare true max attempt is showing a small reserve gap; a large, inconsistent gap between
estimated and tested max may point to arousal/readiness on test day rather than a change
in underlying capacity.

**Related** — [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]].

=================== framework--central-vs-peripheral-fatigue-mechanisms
# Central vs. Peripheral Fatigue, and Low- vs. High-Frequency Fatigue

**What it is** — Fatigue during short-duration strength/power work is split into
**central fatigue** (reduced motivation, impaired spinal nerve transmission, reduced motor
neuron recruitment and firing rate — a CNS-level phenomenon) and **peripheral fatigue**
(failure somewhere in the excitation-contraction chain at the muscle cell itself: motor
end-plate, sarcolemma, T-tubules, sarcoplasmic reticulum, contractile proteins).
Peripheral fatigue further splits into **low-frequency fatigue** (impaired force at <20 Hz
stimulation, from depressed calcium release, with a prolonged recovery period "persisting
for as long as 48 hours," printed 15) and **high-frequency fatigue** (impaired force at
>50 Hz; the text gives no recovery-speed comparison between the two, printed 14-15).
Two distinct purposes are given for reduced central drive during fatigue, on different
pages: for short-term maximal contractions, the reduction in motor-neuron firing rate "may
be beneficial in avoiding electrical failure and facilitating maximal mechanical response"
(printed 15); separately, "muscle wisdom," the CNS's down-regulation of motor neuron
discharge rate during a sustained contraction, has a purpose "believed to ensure that
central neural drive to fatigued skeletal muscle matches that which is needed to generate
the required force," and "may be one mechanism that functions either to decrease or to
postpone central neural fatigue" (printed 16). Exercise-induced ammonia accumulation is
cited as a possible contributor to central fatigue at high intensities/durations. Intensive
CNS activation (max weights, max power, plyometrics) is stated to need at least 48 hours of
recovery if no restorative methods are used. (PDF pp. 24-27, printed pp. 13-16.)

**Why it works** — Fatigue is not a single process with one cause; the central/peripheral
split and the frequency-dependent split reflect genuinely different physiological
bottlenecks (nervous drive vs. contractile-machinery failure vs. calcium-handling
kinetics), which is why they have different time courses and respond to different
recovery strategies.

**When to apply** — The authors state intensive CNS activation (max weights, max power,
plyometrics) needs at least 48 hours of recovery if no restorative methods are used (PDF p.
26, printed p. 15). **Inference:** this supports spacing high-CNS-cost sessions (max
strength, high-velocity work) at least two days apart within a microcycle, and treating
"still feels flat two days after a max-effort day" as plausible central fatigue rather than
assuming poor effort or motivation; this specific practical framing is not stated in the
text.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a mechanistic taxonomy from exercise
physiology, not a monitoring protocol. **Eric's baseline:** modified reactive strength
index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing is the department's chosen daily readiness marker
(`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing
`2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`); **Inference:** mRSI is a downstream readiness proxy,
not a direct central/peripheral fatigue assay, so a flat CMJ day should not be
over-attributed to a specific named mechanism (e.g., "low-frequency fatigue") without EMG
or stimulation data — neither source states this equivalence, and this caution is this
entry's own judgment.

**Example** — Inference: a depressed CMJ the day after max squats more likely reflects
residual fatigue than lost strength; retest at 48 hours rather than reacting to a single
depressed value.

**Related** — [[framework--factors-limiting-strength-production]].

=================== framework--factors-limiting-strength-production
# Seven Factors That Limit Strength Production

**What it is** — Strength output in the short and long term is limited by seven
interacting factors: **trainability** (genetic ceiling for hypertrophy, fibre-type
distribution, leverage, and pre-training status); **neuromuscular efficiency** (skill in
recruiting the right muscles accurately and powerfully); **biomechanical efficiency**
(leverage and relative muscle-group strength, trainable unlike raw genetic trainability);
**psychological factors** (motivation, focus, pain tolerance, perceived exertion, coach
influence); **pain and fear of pain** (distinguishing injury pain, a protective signal to
act on, from effort pain, a subjective load-intensity signal usable via an RPE-style
scale); **injury and fear of injury** (reflex inhibition of contraction around a damaged
joint is well documented; return to top performance depends on the athlete's own
perception that rehab is complete, not just medical clearance); and **fatigue** (central
vs. peripheral, discussed further in
[[framework--central-vs-peripheral-fatigue-mechanisms]]). (PDF pp. 23-24, printed pp.
12-13.)

**Why it works** — Strength testing and training programs typically control for load,
volume, and technique, but this list makes explicit that psychological state, injury
history, and perceived pain/fear operate as real physiological limiters on force output.
Reflex inhibition around an injured joint is stated in the text as "a well-known phenomenon
which produces muscle weakness when a joint is damaged" (Stokes & Young, 1984; printed 14).
Inference: this is not just a "mental" factor layered on top of a physical ceiling, but a
measurable neuromuscular effect, not a motivation problem.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a checklist when an athlete's force output
underperforms their apparent physical capacity: before assuming a physical/programming
cause, rule out fear of re-injury, unaddressed effort-pain tolerance, or psychological
state. The authors state "return to top level performance will occur only if the
athlete perceives rehabilitation to be complete" and the fear of pain or re-injury being
minimal (PDF p. 25, printed p. 14). **Eric's baseline:** Applied Performance's stated role
in return-to-performance is to supply information supporting Athletic Performance's and
Athletic Medicine's RTP decisions, a support/advisory role rather than a final-decision
role (`method-baseline.md`, "Rehab and return to play," citing
`baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6`); that same baseline section is flagged as
"the thinnest discipline in the corpus" with no stated RTP criteria or battery.
**Inference:** the authors' fear-of-injury/pain framing is a plausible partial fill for
that documented gap, though neither source states this connection directly.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a descriptive taxonomy, not a measurement
protocol; none of these seven factors have a given cutoff or test threshold in this section
of the text (PDF pp. 23-24, printed pp. 12-13). **Inference:** do not use "fear of injury"
as a catch-all explanation without other supporting evidence (movement quality, self-report,
clinical input from Athletic Medicine); reflex inhibition and psychological guarding can
look similar from the outside. This caution is this entry's own judgment, not stated in the
text.

**Example** — **Inference:** An athlete cleared medically after an ACL reconstruction who still shows
reduced force output on the operated leg during testing may be exhibiting reflex inhibition
and/or fear of re-injury, not a residual physical deficit alone; that changes what the
next intervention should target.

**Related** — [[framework--central-vs-peripheral-fatigue-mechanisms]].

=================== framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing
# The Two-Factor Model Can Be Formalized Mathematically, and Its Research Base Argues Against Heavy Training Right Before Competition

**What it is** — The Two-Factor (Fitness-Fatigue) Model treats preparedness at time t as
initial preparedness plus the summed effect of a slow-decaying fitness after-effect and a
faster-decaying fatigue after-effect, each with its own magnitude and decay-time constant
(Banister et al., 1992). Banister and Calvert (1980) originated this with the Training
Impulse (TRIMP), a quantified unit of training load used to model and predict elite
swimming performance from the fitness/fatigue balance. Zatsiorsky (1995) is cited for the
same 3:1 fitness-to-fatigue decay ratio already in this library's Bompa material. Later
research building on this model examined tapering specifically: Fitz-Clarke et al. (1991)
found presently accepted taper protocols may be too rigorous and short for best results,
and several studies (Zarkadas et al. 1995; Mujika et al. 1996; Shepley et al. 1992) found
that proper placement of training volume during a taper is a key optimization factor, with
high training volume in the days immediately preceding competition possibly detrimental to
performance. Different muscle groups recover heterochronically, which is why some Russian
restoration specialists deliberately avoid applying restorative methods (e.g. massage) to
every muscle group after every session, since supercompensation is reportedly more
pronounced with partial rather than total restoration. (PDF pp. 99-100, printed pp. 88-89.)

**Why it works** — Modeling preparedness as the sum of two exponentially-decaying
after-effects with different time constants gives periodization a quantitative structure
(not just a qualitative "wave" description), which is what allows taper researchers to ask
a specific, testable question: how much and how recently loaded should training be before
competition to maximize the fitness-minus-fatigue difference at competition time.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this is the more technical, equation-based underpinning
of this library's already-captured practical rule
([[periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]]); cite this entry when a
more rigorous or quantitative framing is needed (e.g. explaining the model to a sport
scientist or in a research-facing document), and cite the Bompa heuristic for the everyday
coaching rule of thumb. The taper-volume finding directly supports reducing training
volume, not just intensity, in the days immediately before a competition or key testing
date.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the specific mathematical constants (A, B, T1, T2)
must be fit per individual and per training phase, and the text notes they require
periodic re-estimation; do not treat this as a plug-and-play formula without that
fitting process. Inference: the cited taper studies are 1990s endurance-sport studies
(Shepley et al. 1992, middle-distance runners; Zarkadas et al. 1995, triathletes; Mujika et
al. 1996, swimmers; the text itself does not name the sports studied); don't assume the
exact taper-volume findings transfer unchanged to football or other team sports without
independent verification.

**Example** — **Inference:** rather than assuming a flat "taper week" cuts intensity but
keeps volume similar, this model's logic and the cited taper research both point toward
deliberately reducing volume (not just easing intensity) in the final days before a key
competition or test date, to let the longer-lasting fitness effect show through as the
shorter fatigue effect clears.

**Related** — [[periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]],
[[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]].

=================== framework--functional-vs-structural-resistance-training
# Functional vs. Structural Resistance Training

**What it is** — Two basic categories of resistance training effect: structural training
targets muscle hypertrophy (and some tissue flexibility); functional training targets
performance qualities (static strength, speed-strength, muscular endurance, reactive
ability) through four neural mechanisms: (1) intermuscular coordination — sequencing and
synchronizing action between different muscle groups; (2) intramuscular coordination —
control within one muscle via number encoding (how many fibres are recruited), rate
encoding (firing frequency), and pattern encoding (sequencing of fibre types); (3)

=================== framework--sarcomere-vs-sarcoplasmic-hypertrophy
# Sarcomere Hypertrophy (Functional) vs. Sarcoplasmic Hypertrophy (Non-Functional)

**What it is** — Two distinct types of muscle hypertrophy are described. Sarcomere
hypertrophy: an increase in the size and number of sarcomeres within myofibrils; when
added in parallel (not just in series) this increases the muscle's cross-sectional density
of contractile tissue and produces a real increase in strength. Sarcoplasmic hypertrophy:
an increase in the volume of non-contractile protein and semifluid plasma between fibres;
cross-sectional area increases, but the density of contractile tissue per unit area
decreases, with no corresponding strength increase. Except in sports where added bodymass
itself matters (bodybuilding, sumo), sarcomere hypertrophy is described as far more
important for athletic performance. Longer, more strenuous submaximal loading (not rapid,
near-maximal, low-repetition loading like Olympic weightlifting) is associated with more
sarcoplasmic and less sarcomere hypertrophy; high-repetition, moderate-resistance training
(bodybuilding/circuit-style) can also make fast-twitch fibres behave more like slow-twitch
fibres (printed 69). (PDF pp. 77-80, printed pp. 66-69.)

This entry is rated `contested` rather than `supported`: the text's own When NOT section
below notes the sarcomere/sarcoplasm distinction is not definitively confirmed, and modern
work argues evidence for sarcoplasmic hypertrophy occurring without a matching strength
gain is limited and mixed (Roberts, Haun et al. 2020, "Sarcoplasmic hypertrophy in skeletal
muscle: a scientific 'unicorn' or resistance training adaptation?", Front Physiol 11:816).

**Why it works** — The two hypertrophy types build different cellular components (more
contractile machinery per fibre vs. more non-contractile fluid/protein volume around
existing machinery), so they produce different ratios of size gain to strength gain
depending on the loading style that stimulated them.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** relevant to explaining why an athlete can add
measurable muscle mass/girth from high-volume, moderate-load training without a
proportionate strength increase, and why weightlifting-style low-rep, high-intensity work
is more strength-efficient per unit of added mass than bodybuilding-style volume training.
Useful framing for a strength coach deciding whether a hypertrophy block should be
biased toward heavier, lower-rep work (sarcomere-biased) or higher-volume work
(sarcoplasm-biased), depending on whether the goal is functional strength or added bodymass
for a specific position.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the exact biochemical trigger for hypertrophy is
stated in the text as not fully known, and this sarcomere/sarcoplasm distinction, while
still commonly discussed, has not been definitively confirmed by direct human
biopsy/histology consensus in the broader literature since; treat it as a useful coaching
model, not a settled biochemical fact, and don't claim a specific training protocol
produces "only" one type of hypertrophy in isolation.

**Example** — **Inference:** a lineman training for added mass and positional strength
might justifiably include both rep ranges, but should not assume high-rep hypertrophy
volume alone will translate proportionally into functional strength gains without
lower-rep, higher-intensity work also present in the program.

# Central vs. Peripheral Fatigue, and Low- vs. High-Frequency Fatigue

**What it is** — Fatigue during short-duration strength/power work is split into
**central fatigue** (reduced motivation, impaired spinal nerve transmission, reduced motor
neuron recruitment and firing rate — a CNS-level phenomenon) and **peripheral fatigue**
(failure somewhere in the excitation-contraction chain at the muscle cell itself: motor
end-plate, sarcolemma, T-tubules, sarcoplasmic reticulum, contractile proteins).
Peripheral fatigue further splits into **low-frequency fatigue** (impaired force at <20 Hz
stimulation, from depressed calcium release, with a prolonged recovery period "persisting
for as long as 48 hours," printed 15) and **high-frequency fatigue** (impaired force at
>50 Hz; the text gives no recovery-speed comparison between the two, printed 14-15).
Two distinct purposes are given for reduced central drive during fatigue, on different
pages: for short-term maximal contractions, the reduction in motor-neuron firing rate "may
be beneficial in avoiding electrical failure and facilitating maximal mechanical response"
(printed 15); separately, "muscle wisdom," the CNS's down-regulation of motor neuron
discharge rate during a sustained contraction, has a purpose "believed to ensure that
central neural drive to fatigued skeletal muscle matches that which is needed to generate
the required force," and "may be one mechanism that functions either to decrease or to
postpone central neural fatigue" (printed 16). Exercise-induced ammonia accumulation is

kinetics), which is why they have different time courses and respond to different
recovery strategies.

# Seven Factors That Limit Strength Production

**What it is** — Strength output in the short and long term is limited by seven
interacting factors: **trainability** (genetic ceiling for hypertrophy, fibre-type
distribution, leverage, and pre-training status); **neuromuscular efficiency** (skill in
recruiting the right muscles accurately and powerfully); **biomechanical efficiency**
(leverage and relative muscle-group strength, trainable unlike raw genetic trainability);
**psychological factors** (motivation, focus, pain tolerance, perceived exertion, coach
influence); **pain and fear of pain** (distinguishing injury pain, a protective signal to
act on, from effort pain, a subjective load-intensity signal usable via an RPE-style
scale); **injury and fear of injury** (reflex inhibition of contraction around a damaged
joint is well documented; return to top performance depends on the athlete's own
perception that rehab is complete, not just medical clearance); and **fatigue** (central

volume, and technique, but this list makes explicit that psychological state, injury
history, and perceived pain/fear operate as real physiological limiters on force output.

=================== framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing
# The Two-Factor Model Can Be Formalized Mathematically, and Its Research Base Argues Against Heavy Training Right Before Competition

**What it is** — The Two-Factor (Fitness-Fatigue) Model treats preparedness at time t as
initial preparedness plus the summed effect of a slow-decaying fitness after-effect and a
faster-decaying fatigue after-effect, each with its own magnitude and decay-time constant
(Banister et al., 1992). Banister and Calvert (1980) originated this with the Training
Impulse (TRIMP), a quantified unit of training load used to model and predict elite
swimming performance from the fitness/fatigue balance. Zatsiorsky (1995) is cited for the
same 3:1 fitness-to-fatigue decay ratio already in this library's Bompa material. Later
research building on this model examined tapering specifically: Fitz-Clarke et al. (1991)
found presently accepted taper protocols may be too rigorous and short for best results,
and several studies (Zarkadas et al. 1995; Mujika et al. 1996; Shepley et al. 1992) found
that proper placement of training volume during a taper is a key optimization factor, with
high training volume in the days immediately preceding competition possibly detrimental to
performance. Different muscle groups recover heterochronically, which is why some Russian
restoration specialists deliberately avoid applying restorative methods (e.g. massage) to
every muscle group after every session, since supercompensation is reportedly more
pronounced with partial rather than total restoration. (PDF pp. 99-100, printed pp. 88-89.)

**Why it works** — Modeling preparedness as the sum of two exponentially-decaying
after-effects with different time constants gives periodization a quantitative structure
(not just a qualitative "wave" description), which is what allows taper researchers to ask
a specific, testable question: how much and how recently loaded should training be before
competition to maximize the fitness-minus-fatigue difference at competition time.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this is the more technical, equation-based underpinning
of this library's already-captured practical rule
([[periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]]); cite this entry when a
more rigorous or quantitative framing is needed (e.g. explaining the model to a sport
scientist or in a research-facing document), and cite the Bompa heuristic for the everyday
coaching rule of thumb. The taper-volume finding directly supports reducing training
volume, not just intensity, in the days immediately before a competition or key testing
date.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the specific mathematical constants (A, B, T1, T2)
must be fit per individual and per training phase, and the text notes they require
periodic re-estimation; do not treat this as a plug-and-play formula without that
fitting process. Inference: the cited taper studies are 1990s endurance-sport studies
(Shepley et al. 1992, middle-distance runners; Zarkadas et al. 1995, triathletes; Mujika et
al. 1996, swimmers; the text itself does not name the sports studied); don't assume the
exact taper-volume findings transfer unchanged to football or other team sports without
independent verification.

**Example** — **Inference:** rather than assuming a flat "taper week" cuts intensity but
keeps volume similar, this model's logic and the cited taper research both point toward
deliberately reducing volume (not just easing intensity) in the final days before a key
competition or test date, to let the longer-lasting fitness effect show through as the
shorter fatigue effect clears.

flexibility as four independent boxes, this model treats them as vertices whose pairwise
and triple combinations describe most of the specific fitness qualities that actually
appear in sport, with skill/neuromuscular control cutting across all of them. Note: at
printed 92 the text itself calls strength-speed and speed-strength "synonymous with the
ability to develop great power," not two distinct qualities; the strength-speed vs.
speed-strength split already used in
[[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]] is attributed there to
"some authorities" (printed 20), not to this pyramidal model.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful as a master vocabulary/reference when precisely
naming which quality a given test or exercise targets (e.g. distinguishing
"strength-speed" training from "speed-strength" training, or "flexibility-strength" from
plain flexibility), and as a teaching framework (e.g. HHPR 5355) for showing students why
"fitness" is not one thing to test or train, but a structured set of specific,
combinable qualities.

**When NOT to apply** — The text itself calls this model "representational or
descriptive rather than scientifically analytical" and notes it is complicated by other
factors such as quasi-isometric states at very slow speeds (PDF p. 103, printed p. 92);
**Inference:** don't treat it as a validated measurement taxonomy with defined tests for
each named compound quality — most of these terms (e.g. "flexibility-skill") have no
standard test attached in this text.

**Example** — **Inference:** describing an athlete's need as "relative strength-speed"
(power per unit bodymass) rather than just "power" gives a program design target that is
precise about both the force-velocity region and the bodymass constraint, useful for a
weight-class or position-limited athlete.

**Related** — [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]],
[[framework--work-capacity-fitness-preparedness]].

=================== framework--sarcomere-vs-sarcoplasmic-hypertrophy
# Sarcomere Hypertrophy (Functional) vs. Sarcoplasmic Hypertrophy (Non-Functional)

**What it is** — Two distinct types of muscle hypertrophy are described. Sarcomere
hypertrophy: an increase in the size and number of sarcomeres within myofibrils; when
added in parallel (not just in series) this increases the muscle's cross-sectional density
of contractile tissue and produces a real increase in strength. Sarcoplasmic hypertrophy:
an increase in the volume of non-contractile protein and semifluid plasma between fibres;
cross-sectional area increases, but the density of contractile tissue per unit area
decreases, with no corresponding strength increase. Except in sports where added bodymass
itself matters (bodybuilding, sumo), sarcomere hypertrophy is described as far more
important for athletic performance. Longer, more strenuous submaximal loading (not rapid,
near-maximal, low-repetition loading like Olympic weightlifting) is associated with more
sarcoplasmic and less sarcomere hypertrophy; high-repetition, moderate-resistance training
(bodybuilding/circuit-style) can also make fast-twitch fibres behave more like slow-twitch
fibres (printed 69). (PDF pp. 77-80, printed pp. 66-69.)

This entry is rated `contested` rather than `supported`: the text's own When NOT section
below notes the sarcomere/sarcoplasm distinction is not definitively confirmed, and modern
work argues evidence for sarcoplasmic hypertrophy occurring without a matching strength
gain is limited and mixed (Roberts, Haun et al. 2020, "Sarcoplasmic hypertrophy in skeletal
muscle: a scientific 'unicorn' or resistance training adaptation?", Front Physiol 11:816).

**Why it works** — The two hypertrophy types build different cellular components (more
contractile machinery per fibre vs. more non-contractile fluid/protein volume around
existing machinery), so they produce different ratios of size gain to strength gain
depending on the loading style that stimulated them.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** relevant to explaining why an athlete can add
measurable muscle mass/girth from high-volume, moderate-load training without a
proportionate strength increase, and why weightlifting-style low-rep, high-intensity work
is more strength-efficient per unit of added mass than bodybuilding-style volume training.
Useful framing for a strength coach deciding whether a hypertrophy block should be
biased toward heavier, lower-rep work (sarcomere-biased) or higher-volume work
(sarcoplasm-biased), depending on whether the goal is functional strength or added bodymass
for a specific position.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the exact biochemical trigger for hypertrophy is
stated in the text as not fully known, and this sarcomere/sarcoplasm distinction, while
still commonly discussed, has not been definitively confirmed by direct human
biopsy/histology consensus in the broader literature since; treat it as a useful coaching
model, not a settled biochemical fact, and don't claim a specific training protocol
produces "only" one type of hypertrophy in isolation.

**Example** — **Inference:** a lineman training for added mass and positional strength
might justifiably include both rep ranges, but should not assume high-rep hypertrophy
volume alone will translate proportionally into functional strength gains without
lower-rep, higher-intensity work also present in the program.

**Related** — [[claim--continuous-vs-interval-circuit-training-for-concurrent-goals]].

=================== framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components
# The Muscle Model: Series Elastic Component (SEC) vs. Parallel Elastic Component (PEC)

**What it is** — A mechanical model of muscle (Levin & Wyman, 1927) treats it as a
contractile component in series with a Series Elastic Component (SEC: tendon,
cross-bridges, myofilaments, titin, Z-discs) and in parallel with a Parallel Elastic
Component (PEC: sarcolemma, rest-state cross-bridging, surrounding sheaths). The PEC
carries the force of a relaxed muscle stretched beyond resting length, and stores little
usable energy; the SEC is tensioned by an actively contracting muscle resisting a rapid
stretch, and stores considerable elastic energy — this is the mechanism plyometric/shock
training exploits. Slow-twitch (ST) dominant muscle shows smaller mechanical strain when
stretched while contracted but has a stiffer, more elastic SEC than fast-twitch
(FT)-dominant muscle, largely due to higher collagen concentration in slow muscle. The book
gives conflicting statements on which fibre type stores more elastic energy overall:
printed 41 states "the stored elastic energy is greater in FT fibres" (Komi, 1984), while
printed 46 states "a slow muscle can store relatively more elastic energy in its
collagenous tissue than fast muscle." Both are recorded here rather than harmonized.
Static, relaxed, and passive stretching mainly load the PEC; "tense ballistic and active
stretching affects predominantly the SEC," while PNF techniques "appear to be able to
stretch and strengthen both the SEC and the PEC" (printed 41-42). (PDF pp. 51-52, printed
pp. 40-41.)

**Why it works** — Distinguishing which structure (PEC vs. SEC) is under tension during a
given stretch or contraction condition explains why different stretching methods (static
passive vs. active/PNF) target different tissue, and why fast, elastic-energy-storing
tissue (SEC-dominant, FT-rich muscle) behaves differently under rapid loading than slow,
postural (ST-rich, PEC/collagen-dominant) muscle.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful for explaining why plyometric/reactive-strength
training targets the SEC specifically (rapid stretch under active contraction) rather than
simple static flexibility work (which mostly loads the PEC), and for choosing PNF-style
active stretching when the goal is to influence both components rather than the PEC alone.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the anatomical location of SEC/PEC elements is
explicitly stated as not precisely identified (PDF p. 52, printed p. 41); treat this as a
functional/mechanical model for reasoning about elastic energy, not a literal anatomical
map to test or measure directly in an athlete.

**Example** — Inference: by the authors' own account, slow postural muscle needs longer
stretching to meaningfully change its flexibility than fast muscle does (printed 41), which
supports muscle-specific rather than uniform flexibility prescription; this is distinct
from, and does not depend on, the unresolved FT-vs-ST elastic-energy-storage conflict
above.

**Related** — [[claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates]],
[[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]].

=================== framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology
# The Shock Method (Original Russian "Udarnyi Metod"), and Why "Plyometrics" Is a Loose Translation

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky developed the "shock method" (udarnyi metod) as a special
speed-strength training method exploiting connective and elastic tissue's ability to
store and release elastic energy during stretch-shortening of the muscle complex (running,
jumping, throwing, rapid lifting). The rise in concentric strength after rapid "shock"
loading comes from two sources: increased muscle tension from the myotatic (stretch)
reflex, and explosive release of elastic energy stored in connective/elastic tissue during
the eccentric phase. Historically, "pliometric" "was apparently coined to mean eccentric
contraction"; in this scheme of nomenclature (the text does not state it to be
specifically Russian), isometric retained its meaning of static contraction, miometric
meant concentric contraction, and pliometric meant eccentric contraction (printed 34); the
term "plyometrics," as adopted in the West, has drifted to describe a broader category of
jumping drills, many of which do not reproduce true shock-method characteristics. The
text's precise redefinition: the term plyometrics should refer to "an eccentric muscle
contraction ... suddenly terminated in an explosive isometric contraction, thereby
producing a powerful myotatic reflex, a sharp extension of the passive components of the
muscle complex and a subsequent explosive concentric contraction," and "should not refer
to ordinary jumping" (printed 34-35). (PDF pp. 45-46, printed pp. 34-35.)

**Why it works** — Inference: the stretch-shortening cycle mechanism (reflex potentiation
plus elastic energy return) is well established in modern SSC/plyometric research
independent of this text; this entry's contribution is the terminology history and the
precise mechanical definition, which distinguishes genuine shock-method work from
ordinary jumping drills marketed under the same name.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful when auditing whether a program's "plyometric"
exercises actually meet the text's precise definition (a sudden eccentric-to-isometric-
to-concentric sequence) versus being ordinary jump training relabeled; this matters for
predicting whether the intended reactive-strength adaptation is actually being trained.
This library already traces Verkhoshansky's shock-method lineage at a higher level in
[[fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--soviet-lineage-of-sprint-training-ideas|The
Soviet Lineage Behind Modern Sprint-Training Ideas]]; that entry credits him with "shock
method (plyometrics)" but does not cover the terminology history or mechanism given here,
so this entry adds a genuinely new angle rather than duplicating it.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** do not assume every drill called "plyometric" in
current commercial or popular usage (e.g. step-aerobics-style jumping) reproduces the
shock-method mechanism. "Russian scientists prefer to retain the term 'shock method' ...
and 'depth jumps'" (printed 34), while Siff separately proposes "powermetrics" for the
whole collection of jumping and rebound methods (Siff, 1998, printed 35). This terminology
distinction does not itself tell a coach which drills are safe or appropriate for a given
athlete; that is a separate training-age and readiness question.

**Example** — **Inference:** a coach programming "plyometrics" for a novice athlete should
check whether the intended exercise involves a true rapid eccentric-to-concentric shock
transition (a depth jump) or is really just a submaximal hop/jump drill; the two carry very
different neuromuscular demands despite sharing the popular label.

**Related** — [[framework--determinants-of-strength-structural-functional]],
[[fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--soviet-lineage-of-sprint-training-ideas]]
(reciprocal link recommended there: note that Supertraining Ch1.6 gives the
isometric/miometric/pliometric terminology scheme and the precise mechanical definition of
the shock method that this lineage table only names in passing).

=================== framework--types-of-maximal-strength
# Types of Maximal Strength (CFmax, TFmax, Fmm, Relative Strength)

**What it is** — The authors (citing Zatsiorsky) separate "maximum strength" into a
ladder of distinct maxima, from lowest to highest: training maximum (TFmax, the training
1RM, the heaviest load one can lift without a large emotional/heart-rate spike),
competitive maximum (CFmax, the true 1RM produced under optimal competitive motivation),
and absolute strength (Fmm, "maximum of all maxima," the involuntary ceiling reachable
only under electrical stimulation or a sudden reflex-recruited load, e.g. a sudden drop
or stretch reflex). Relative strength is strength per unit bodymass for a given lift.
Voluntary maxima also rank by contraction type, in order of magnitude: eccentric >
isometric > concentric. (PDF pp. 12-13, printed pp. 1-2.)

**Why it works** — Nervous system inhibition (protective feedback, comparable to a
mechanical governor) normally prevents a muscle from contracting to the point of
structural failure. Competitive arousal and motivation reduce that inhibition further
than routine training effort does, which is why CFmax exceeds TFmax; involuntary or
reflex-driven recruitment removes still more of it, which is why Fmm exceeds CFmax.

**When to apply** — The authors state the competitive maximum, not the daily training
maximum, should set %-based intensity zones for higher-level athletes, because CFmax stays
comparatively stable while TFmax fluctuates day to day (PDF p. 13, printed p. 2).
**Inference:** this ladder is a useful lens for deciding which measured maximum should
anchor programmed intensity for a given athlete. **Eric's baseline:** velocity-based 1RM
estimation (linear-displacement transducer, target mean velocity) is preferred over live
1RM attempts to avoid the fatigue and injury risk of true maxing (`method-baseline.md`,
"Testing and assessment," citing `ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md`; flagged there as
"Inferred (author uncertain — legacy protocol)," and that same Assessment Manual is
separately flagged as likely outdated since it is built around GymAware, not the current
Perch-centered stack). **Inference:** that preference is consistent with this framework's
logic of anchoring intensity to a stable maximum rather than a noisy daily one, though the
baseline document does not itself cite Zatsiorsky's TFmax/CFmax terminology, and Perch is
not itself named in the baseline material as the current 1RM-estimation tool.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a terminology and reasoning framework, not a measured
protocol; Fmm requires electrical stimulation or reflex loading, which the text
calls impractical (PDF p. 12, printed p. 1). **Inference:** none of these four
maxima are named as routinely and directly measured in Baylor's own documented protocols
(`method-baseline.md`), so this should be treated as a mental model for why training-day
and competition-day 1RMs diverge, not as a set of numbers to test for. The text gives the
eccentric > isometric > concentric ordering "as a matter of interest" (printed 2) without
stating it is a fixed ratio; Inference: it likely varies by joint angle, velocity, and
muscle group, though the text does not make that qualification in this passage.

**Example** — **Inference:** An athlete's best training-day squat (TFmax) is consistently lower than
what they hit in a max-out competition or meet (CFmax); programming off the meet number
rather than a re-tested gym max avoids under-loading the athlete for weeks after a strong
competitive performance.

**Related** — [[claim--voluntary-involuntary-strength-reserve-magnitudes]] (the numeric
gaps between these maxima); [[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]]
(a practical field proxy for the same voluntary/involuntary gap).

=================== heuristic--plan-variation-to-avoid-restrictive-neural-patterns
# Restrictive, Repetitive Patterns May Overspecialize the Nervous System

**What it is** — Drawing on neuroplasticity research (Rosenzweig, Diamond, Greenough,
cortical reorganization in amputees and stroke patients), the text argues the nervous
system rewires quickly (within minutes, not years) around whatever movement pattern is
repeated, and lists practical inferences: avoid machines that restrict joint movement to
one plane/pattern (they can reprogram the brain toward that restricted pattern and reduce
sport-specific capability); avoid over-reliance on ergogenic devices (lifting belts, wrist
wraps, shoe wedges) that can make efficient unassisted movement harder later; favor
planned variation of means, methods, and exercises over fixed repetition of the same
weights or machines; respect individual movement style rather than forcing one stereotyped
technique on every athlete. (PDF pp. 19-20, printed pp. 8-9.)

**Why it works** — Inference: the underlying neuroscience (adult cortical plasticity, rapid
synaptic change, constraint-induced reorganization in rehab patients) is well established.
The extension to healthy-athlete strength training — that machine use or ergogenic aids
will measurably "reprogram" sport-specific neural patterns — is the text's own inference,
not a finding directly tested in athletes in this section.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this can be used as a rationale for favoring
free-weight, multi-planar, compound movement over single-joint machine work when the goal
is direct transfer to a sport skill, and for planning intentional exercise variation
across a training block rather than running the same fixed machine circuit indefinitely.
**Eric's baseline:** the department teaches "knowledge from experience" as an operating
value: keep things simple, teach basic movement skills and basic lifts before anything
advanced, and require bodyweight competency before loaded work
(`method-baseline.md`, "Philosophy and decision principles," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.4-5`, `week1-lecture.md p.12`). **Inference:**
that basic-movement-first philosophy is broadly consistent with this heuristic's caution
about restrictive machine patterns, though the baseline material does not itself cite a
neuroplasticity mechanism or single out machines specifically.

**When NOT to apply** — This entry is rated `contested` where it implies routine machine
use or belts during max lifts causes lasting neural harm to sport skill; the text (PDF pp.
19-20, printed pp. 8-9) gives no dose-response evidence for that extension. The named
counterpoint: injury-prevention evidence for lifting belts is itself weak (e.g. NIOSH,
1994, found insufficient evidence that belts reduce back-injury risk), and studies
comparing machine and free-weight training have found similar strength gains between the
two, which cuts against treating machines as uniquely "restrictive" in outcome terms.
**Inference:** this passage gives no evidence on belts either way; do not use this
heuristic, in either direction, to make a safety claim about belts for heavy compound
lifts.

**Example** — **Inference:** Programming a hip-thrust machine as the sole posterior-chain exercise for a
sprinter, with no free-weight hip hinge or sprint-pattern work anywhere in the week, is the
scenario this heuristic warns against; it does not warn against occasional supported
machine use as part of a varied program.

**Related** — [[framework--functional-vs-structural-resistance-training]].

=================== heuristic--program-variable-complexity-scales-with-training-age
# Beginners Respond to Load Alone; Advanced Athletes Need the Full Variable Set

**What it is** — Load, reps, and sets are described as the traditional core variables of a
weight program, but the text lists a much longer set of variables that matter more as
training age rises: the type of strength fitness required, contraction type, movement
speed by phase, acceleration at critical points, rest interval length and type
(active/passive), exercise sequence,
agonist/antagonist and stabilizer/mover strength balance, static/dynamic range of motion,
individual strength deficit, training history, injury history, and level of sports
proficiency. The proficiency factor is called out as especially important: exact
sequencing of strength, strength-speed, and hypertrophy work barely matters in a
beginner's first weeks/months but matters a great deal for an experienced athlete. Loads
as small as 40% of 1RM can measurably strengthen a beginner but do nothing for an elite
athlete. (PDF pp. 22-23, printed pp. 11-12.)

**Why it works** — The author gives no mechanism. Inference: a novice's nervous system and
tissue are both far from their adaptive ceiling, so almost any consistent stimulus produces
a training effect; an advanced athlete has used up most of that low-hanging adaptive room,
so the remaining gains depend on precisely managing the variables that were negligible for
the novice.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this supports a rule for how much programming detail is
worth the coaching time — spend detailed variable-management effort (sequencing, rest
structure, ROM, asymmetry work) on advanced/experienced athletes, and keep novice
programming simple and consistency-focused. This library's Bompa book makes a related point
from the development-model side ([[periodization--bompa/heuristic--biological-vs-training-age|Biological
vs Chronological vs Training Age]]), though that entry addresses age-grouping and injury
risk rather than this book's programming-variable-complexity angle specifically.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** don't use "they're a beginner" as an excuse to
ignore movement quality, technique, or safety variables; the text's simplification applies
to programming complexity (sequencing, minor load percentages, PDF pp. 22-23, printed pp.
11-12), not to coaching attention on how an exercise is performed — this distinction is
this entry's own reading, not stated explicitly in the text. **Inference:** an older
athlete new to formal training still has a low training age by this logic and should be
treated as a beginner by this rule, not by chronological age; the text does not
draw that chronological-vs-training-age distinction itself in this section.

**Example** — **Inference:** A true freshman gains strength on almost any structured 3x/week program with
straightforward load progression; a fourth-year starter needs exercise sequencing,
recovery structure, and asymmetry correction actively managed to keep progressing.

**Related** — [[framework--resistance-training-prescription-by-goal]].

=================== principle--equal-force-different-loading-methods
# The Same Force (F = ma) Produced Different Ways Trains Differently

**What it is** — Newton's second law (F = ma) means the same force can be produced with a
large mass and small acceleration (powerlifting-style, heavy load), a small mass and large
acceleration (many track and field actions), a moderate mass and moderate acceleration
(bodybuilding-style hypertrophy training, roughly 8-12 reps), or near-zero acceleration
under isometric/isokinetic conditions. Despite equal force output, these methods are
argued and shown in practice not to produce the same training effect, because different
neural, muscular, and metabolic processes are engaged in each case. (PDF pp. 32-33,
printed pp. 21-22.)

**Why it works** — The text bases the "do not produce the same results" claim on "practical
experience from three different competitive aspects of strength training" (powerlifting,
weightlifting, bodybuilding; printed 22), not on a stated mechanism. Inference: force alone
does not specify the movement's velocity, duration, muscle action type, or motor unit
recruitment/firing pattern, all of which independently affect the training stimulus; two
efforts that reach the same peak force via different mass-acceleration combinations are
mechanically equal on that one variable but different on several others that matter
physiologically.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a reasoning check against choosing exercises
solely by "how much force does this produce," when the intended adaptation (max strength
vs. explosive power vs. hypertrophy vs. isometric endurance) requires matching the
mass-acceleration profile, not just the force magnitude, to the target quality. This
generalized application is this entry's own extension of the four loading-option
comparison (PDF pp. 32-33, printed pp. 21-22).

**When NOT to apply** — The authors state isokinetic training (option d, F = k.R)
correlates poorly with actual sporting performance despite producing meaningful
non-specific strength gains in a lab setting (PDF p. 33, printed p. 22, citing Rosentzweig
& Hinson 1972, Ostemig 1986). **Inference:** don't treat isokinetic results as a proxy for
how an athlete will perform in ballistic, free-loading sport actions; this specific
caution is this entry's own restatement of that finding's practical implication.
Inference: for hypertrophy specifically, load magnitude matters less than effort: similar
hypertrophy is reported across a wide load range when sets are taken to failure (Schoenfeld
et al. 2017, JSCR), so the "do not produce the same results" claim is more load-outcome-
specific than the text's general statement suggests.

**Example** — **Inference:** A powerlifting-style heavy squat and an Olympic-style ballistic
clean pull can both produce a similar peak force at the bar, but the clean pull's high
acceleration under a lighter relative load trains rate of force development and ballistic
coordination that the heavy, slow squat does not, and vice versa for maximal-tension
adaptation.

**Related** — [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]].
confidence: supported
=================== principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity
# The Force-Velocity Relationship, and Why Strength Doesn't Guarantee Speed

**What it is** — Hill's hyperbolic force-velocity curve: velocity of contraction is
inversely related to load; large force cannot be produced at very high velocities under
constant conditions; heavy strength training shifts the curve upward, particularly in
beginners (raising force at all velocities, called training for "strength-speed"); light,
high-velocity training shifts the curve's velocity maximum rightward (called training for
"speed-strength"). Because power = force x velocity, both shifts raise power, just at
different points on the curve. Zatsiorsky (1995) reports "there is no correlation between
maximal velocity and maximal strength" (printed 20); the ability to generate maximum
strength and to produce high speed are described as different motor abilities. Inference:
this specific claim is contested by modern data (Wisloff et al. 2004, Br J Sports Med
38:285, squat 1RM vs. 10 m sprint time, r ~0.94; Seitz et al. 2014, Sports Med, strength
gains transferring to sprint performance). (PDF pp. 30-31, printed pp. 19-20; Zatsiorsky &
Matveev 1964, Komi 1979, Zatsiorsky 1995.)

**Why it works** — The Hill curve, "although this relationship originally was derived for
isolated muscle, ... has been confirmed for actual sporting movement" (printed 19). Beyond
that author's statement, the rest is Inference: the F-V relationship reflects the
cross-bridge cycling and motor unit recruitment limits of muscle contraction, and is the
conceptual ancestor of the force-velocity profiling methods (Samozino, Morin, and others)
used in modern sprint and jump testing; the book does not itself draw that connection to
modern profiling.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** justifies programming that targets a specific region of
the force-velocity spectrum rather than assuming "more strength" automatically transfers to
speed: heavy-load, low-velocity work develops the force end; light-load, high-velocity
(including ballistic/plyometric) work develops the velocity end. **Inference:** usable as
the conceptual basis for choosing between a strength-speed or speed-strength emphasis block
for an athlete whose limiter has been identified (e.g., via jump testing or sprint
force-velocity profiling); this specific screening application is not stated in the text.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** don't treat "no correlation between max strength and
max velocity" (PDF p. 31, printed p. 20) as license to ignore strength training for a
speed-limited athlete; a certain strength floor is plausibly still necessary before
speed-specific training pays off. **Eric's baseline:** the Vermeil hierarchy of athletic
development (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill) is
repeatedly described as the department's programming "compass" (`method-baseline.md`,
"Strength and power," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.9-10,18-19`).
**Inference:** that sequencing is broadly consistent with treating a strength floor as a
prerequisite, though neither this text's cited section nor the baseline states the two
frameworks are equivalent. The text itself flags the classic hyperbolic F-V curve as not
universally accurate: research on the lumbar erector spinae shows a "yielding" drop in
force during constant-velocity eccentric stretching that the standard curve doesn't predict
(Sutarno & McGill, 1995; PDF p. 30, printed p. 19) — the model is a strong generalization,
not a universal law for every muscle group.

**Example** — **Inference:** Two athletes with equal back squat 1RM (similar max force) can have very
different unloaded sprint speeds; that gap is F-V curve position, not raw strength, and
argues for velocity-end training (sprint work, light-load ballistics) rather than more
heavy squatting to close it.

**Related** — [[principle--torque-optimization-in-lifting-technique]],
[[principle--equal-force-different-loading-methods]].

stretch, and stores considerable elastic energy — this is the mechanism plyometric/shock
training exploits. Slow-twitch (ST) dominant muscle shows smaller mechanical strain when
stretched while contracted but has a stiffer, more elastic SEC than fast-twitch
(FT)-dominant muscle, largely due to higher collagen concentration in slow muscle. The book
gives conflicting statements on which fibre type stores more elastic energy overall:
printed 41 states "the stored elastic energy is greater in FT fibres" (Komi, 1984), while
printed 46 states "a slow muscle can store relatively more elastic energy in its
collagenous tissue than fast muscle." Both are recorded here rather than harmonized.
Static, relaxed, and passive stretching mainly load the PEC; "tense ballistic and active
stretching affects predominantly the SEC," while PNF techniques "appear to be able to
stretch and strengthen both the SEC and the PEC" (printed 41-42). (PDF pp. 51-52, printed
pp. 40-41.)

**Why it works** — Distinguishing which structure (PEC vs. SEC) is under tension during a
given stretch or contraction condition explains why different stretching methods (static
passive vs. active/PNF) target different tissue, and why fast, elastic-energy-storing
tissue (SEC-dominant, FT-rich muscle) behaves differently under rapid loading than slow,
postural (ST-rich, PEC/collagen-dominant) muscle.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful for explaining why plyometric/reactive-strength
training targets the SEC specifically (rapid stretch under active contraction) rather than
simple static flexibility work (which mostly loads the PEC), and for choosing PNF-style
active stretching when the goal is to influence both components rather than the PEC alone.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the anatomical location of SEC/PEC elements is
explicitly stated as not precisely identified (PDF p. 52, printed p. 41); treat this as a
functional/mechanical model for reasoning about elastic energy, not a literal anatomical
map to test or measure directly in an athlete.

**Example** — Inference: by the authors' own account, slow postural muscle needs longer
stretching to meaningfully change its flexibility than fast muscle does (printed 41), which
supports muscle-specific rather than uniform flexibility prescription; this is distinct
from, and does not depend on, the unresolved FT-vs-ST elastic-energy-storage conflict
above.

**Related** — [[claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates]],
[[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]].
confidence: supported
=================== framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology
# The Shock Method (Original Russian "Udarnyi Metod"), and Why "Plyometrics" Is a Loose Translation

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky developed the "shock method" (udarnyi metod) as a special
speed-strength training method exploiting connective and elastic tissue's ability to
store and release elastic energy during stretch-shortening of the muscle complex (running,
jumping, throwing, rapid lifting). The rise in concentric strength after rapid "shock"
loading comes from two sources: increased muscle tension from the myotatic (stretch)
reflex, and explosive release of elastic energy stored in connective/elastic tissue during
the eccentric phase. Historically, "pliometric" "was apparently coined to mean eccentric
contraction"; in this scheme of nomenclature (the text does not state it to be
specifically Russian), isometric retained its meaning of static contraction, miometric
meant concentric contraction, and pliometric meant eccentric contraction (printed 34); the
term "plyometrics," as adopted in the West, has drifted to describe a broader category of
jumping drills, many of which do not reproduce true shock-method characteristics. The
text's precise redefinition: the term plyometrics should refer to "an eccentric muscle
contraction ... suddenly terminated in an explosive isometric contraction, thereby
producing a powerful myotatic reflex, a sharp extension of the passive components of the
muscle complex and a subsequent explosive concentric contraction," and "should not refer
to ordinary jumping" (printed 34-35). (PDF pp. 45-46, printed pp. 34-35.)

**Why it works** — Inference: the stretch-shortening cycle mechanism (reflex potentiation
plus elastic energy return) is well established in modern SSC/plyometric research
independent of this text; this entry's contribution is the terminology history and the
precise mechanical definition, which distinguishes genuine shock-method work from
ordinary jumping drills marketed under the same name.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful when auditing whether a program's "plyometric"
exercises actually meet the text's precise definition (a sudden eccentric-to-isometric-
to-concentric sequence) versus being ordinary jump training relabeled; this matters for
predicting whether the intended reactive-strength adaptation is actually being trained.
This library already traces Verkhoshansky's shock-method lineage at a higher level in
[[fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--soviet-lineage-of-sprint-training-ideas|The
Soviet Lineage Behind Modern Sprint-Training Ideas]]; that entry credits him with "shock
method (plyometrics)" but does not cover the terminology history or mechanism given here,
so this entry adds a genuinely new angle rather than duplicating it.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** do not assume every drill called "plyometric" in
current commercial or popular usage (e.g. step-aerobics-style jumping) reproduces the
shock-method mechanism. "Russian scientists prefer to retain the term 'shock method' ...
and 'depth jumps'" (printed 34), while Siff separately proposes "powermetrics" for the
whole collection of jumping and rebound methods (Siff, 1998, printed 35). This terminology
distinction does not itself tell a coach which drills are safe or appropriate for a given
athlete; that is a separate training-age and readiness question.

**Example** — **Inference:** a coach programming "plyometrics" for a novice athlete should
check whether the intended exercise involves a true rapid eccentric-to-concentric shock
transition (a depth jump) or is really just a submaximal hop/jump drill; the two carry very
different neuromuscular demands despite sharing the popular label.

**Related** — [[framework--determinants-of-strength-structural-functional]],
[[fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--soviet-lineage-of-sprint-training-ideas]]
(reciprocal link recommended there: note that Supertraining Ch1.6 gives the
isometric/miometric/pliometric terminology scheme and the precise mechanical definition of
the shock method that this lineage table only names in passing).

=================== framework--types-of-maximal-strength
# Types of Maximal Strength (CFmax, TFmax, Fmm, Relative Strength)

**What it is** — The authors (citing Zatsiorsky) separate "maximum strength" into a
ladder of distinct maxima, from lowest to highest: training maximum (TFmax, the training
1RM, the heaviest load one can lift without a large emotional/heart-rate spike),
competitive maximum (CFmax, the true 1RM produced under optimal competitive motivation),
and absolute strength (Fmm, "maximum of all maxima," the involuntary ceiling reachable
only under electrical stimulation or a sudden reflex-recruited load, e.g. a sudden drop
or stretch reflex). Relative strength is strength per unit bodymass for a given lift.
Voluntary maxima also rank by contraction type, in order of magnitude: eccentric >
isometric > concentric. (PDF pp. 12-13, printed pp. 1-2.)

**Why it works** — Nervous system inhibition (protective feedback, comparable to a
mechanical governor) normally prevents a muscle from contracting to the point of
structural failure. Competitive arousal and motivation reduce that inhibition further
than routine training effort does, which is why CFmax exceeds TFmax; involuntary or
reflex-driven recruitment removes still more of it, which is why Fmm exceeds CFmax.

**When to apply** — The authors state the competitive maximum, not the daily training
maximum, should set %-based intensity zones for higher-level athletes, because CFmax stays
comparatively stable while TFmax fluctuates day to day (PDF p. 13, printed p. 2).
**Inference:** this ladder is a useful lens for deciding which measured maximum should
anchor programmed intensity for a given athlete. **Eric's baseline:** velocity-based 1RM
estimation (linear-displacement transducer, target mean velocity) is preferred over live
1RM attempts to avoid the fatigue and injury risk of true maxing (`method-baseline.md`,
"Testing and assessment," citing `ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md`; flagged there as
"Inferred (author uncertain — legacy protocol)," and that same Assessment Manual is
separately flagged as likely outdated since it is built around GymAware, not the current
Perch-centered stack). **Inference:** that preference is consistent with this framework's
logic of anchoring intensity to a stable maximum rather than a noisy daily one, though the
baseline document does not itself cite Zatsiorsky's TFmax/CFmax terminology, and Perch is
not itself named in the baseline material as the current 1RM-estimation tool.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a terminology and reasoning framework, not a measured
protocol; Fmm requires electrical stimulation or reflex loading, which the text
calls impractical (PDF p. 12, printed p. 1). **Inference:** none of these four
maxima are named as routinely and directly measured in Baylor's own documented protocols
(`method-baseline.md`), so this should be treated as a mental model for why training-day
and competition-day 1RMs diverge, not as a set of numbers to test for. The text gives the
eccentric > isometric > concentric ordering "as a matter of interest" (printed 2) without
stating it is a fixed ratio; Inference: it likely varies by joint angle, velocity, and
muscle group, though the text does not make that qualification in this passage.

**Example** — **Inference:** An athlete's best training-day squat (TFmax) is consistently lower than
what they hit in a max-out competition or meet (CFmax); programming off the meet number
rather than a re-tested gym max avoids under-loading the athlete for weeks after a strong
competitive performance.

**Related** — [[claim--voluntary-involuntary-strength-reserve-magnitudes]] (the numeric
gaps between these maxima); [[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]]
(a practical field proxy for the same voluntary/involuntary gap).

=================== heuristic--plan-variation-to-avoid-restrictive-neural-patterns
# Restrictive, Repetitive Patterns May Overspecialize the Nervous System

**What it is** — Drawing on neuroplasticity research (Rosenzweig, Diamond, Greenough,
cortical reorganization in amputees and stroke patients), the text argues the nervous
system rewires quickly (within minutes, not years) around whatever movement pattern is
repeated, and lists practical inferences: avoid machines that restrict joint movement to
one plane/pattern (they can reprogram the brain toward that restricted pattern and reduce
sport-specific capability); avoid over-reliance on ergogenic devices (lifting belts, wrist
wraps, shoe wedges) that can make efficient unassisted movement harder later; favor
planned variation of means, methods, and exercises over fixed repetition of the same
weights or machines; respect individual movement style rather than forcing one stereotyped
technique on every athlete. (PDF pp. 19-20, printed pp. 8-9.)

**Why it works** — Inference: the underlying neuroscience (adult cortical plasticity, rapid
synaptic change, constraint-induced reorganization in rehab patients) is well established.
The extension to healthy-athlete strength training — that machine use or ergogenic aids
will measurably "reprogram" sport-specific neural patterns — is the text's own inference,
not a finding directly tested in athletes in this section.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this can be used as a rationale for favoring
free-weight, multi-planar, compound movement over single-joint machine work when the goal
is direct transfer to a sport skill, and for planning intentional exercise variation
across a training block rather than running the same fixed machine circuit indefinitely.
**Eric's baseline:** the department teaches "knowledge from experience" as an operating
value: keep things simple, teach basic movement skills and basic lifts before anything
advanced, and require bodyweight competency before loaded work
(`method-baseline.md`, "Philosophy and decision principles," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.4-5`, `week1-lecture.md p.12`). **Inference:**
that basic-movement-first philosophy is broadly consistent with this heuristic's caution
about restrictive machine patterns, though the baseline material does not itself cite a
neuroplasticity mechanism or single out machines specifically.

**When NOT to apply** — This entry is rated `contested` where it implies routine machine
use or belts during max lifts causes lasting neural harm to sport skill; the text (PDF pp.
19-20, printed pp. 8-9) gives no dose-response evidence for that extension. The named
counterpoint: injury-prevention evidence for lifting belts is itself weak (e.g. NIOSH,
1994, found insufficient evidence that belts reduce back-injury risk), and studies
comparing machine and free-weight training have found similar strength gains between the
two, which cuts against treating machines as uniquely "restrictive" in outcome terms.
**Inference:** this passage gives no evidence on belts either way; do not use this
heuristic, in either direction, to make a safety claim about belts for heavy compound
lifts.

**Example** — **Inference:** Programming a hip-thrust machine as the sole posterior-chain exercise for a
sprinter, with no free-weight hip hinge or sprint-pattern work anywhere in the week, is the
scenario this heuristic warns against; it does not warn against occasional supported
machine use as part of a varied program.

**Related** — [[framework--functional-vs-structural-resistance-training]].

=================== heuristic--program-variable-complexity-scales-with-training-age
# Beginners Respond to Load Alone; Advanced Athletes Need the Full Variable Set

**What it is** — Load, reps, and sets are described as the traditional core variables of a
weight program, but the text lists a much longer set of variables that matter more as
training age rises: the type of strength fitness required, contraction type, movement
speed by phase, acceleration at critical points, rest interval length and type
(active/passive), exercise sequence,
agonist/antagonist and stabilizer/mover strength balance, static/dynamic range of motion,
individual strength deficit, training history, injury history, and level of sports
proficiency. The proficiency factor is called out as especially important: exact
sequencing of strength, strength-speed, and hypertrophy work barely matters in a
beginner's first weeks/months but matters a great deal for an experienced athlete. Loads
as small as 40% of 1RM can measurably strengthen a beginner but do nothing for an elite
athlete. (PDF pp. 22-23, printed pp. 11-12.)

**Why it works** — The author gives no mechanism. Inference: a novice's nervous system and
tissue are both far from their adaptive ceiling, so almost any consistent stimulus produces
a training effect; an advanced athlete has used up most of that low-hanging adaptive room,
so the remaining gains depend on precisely managing the variables that were negligible for
the novice.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this supports a rule for how much programming detail is
worth the coaching time — spend detailed variable-management effort (sequencing, rest
structure, ROM, asymmetry work) on advanced/experienced athletes, and keep novice
programming simple and consistency-focused. This library's Bompa book makes a related point
from the development-model side ([[periodization--bompa/heuristic--biological-vs-training-age|Biological
vs Chronological vs Training Age]]), though that entry addresses age-grouping and injury
risk rather than this book's programming-variable-complexity angle specifically.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** don't use "they're a beginner" as an excuse to
ignore movement quality, technique, or safety variables; the text's simplification applies
to programming complexity (sequencing, minor load percentages, PDF pp. 22-23, printed pp.
11-12), not to coaching attention on how an exercise is performed — this distinction is
this entry's own reading, not stated explicitly in the text. **Inference:** an older
athlete new to formal training still has a low training age by this logic and should be
treated as a beginner by this rule, not by chronological age; the text does not
draw that chronological-vs-training-age distinction itself in this section.

**Example** — **Inference:** A true freshman gains strength on almost any structured 3x/week program with
straightforward load progression; a fourth-year starter needs exercise sequencing,
recovery structure, and asymmetry correction actively managed to keep progressing.

**Related** — [[framework--resistance-training-prescription-by-goal]].
