=================== principle--equal-force-different-loading-methods
# The Same Force (F = ma) Produced Different Ways Trains Differently

**What it is** — Newton's second law (F = ma) means the same force can be produced with a
large mass and small acceleration (powerlifting-style, heavy load), a small mass and large
acceleration (many track and field actions), a moderate mass and moderate acceleration
(bodybuilding-style hypertrophy training, roughly 8-12 reps), or near-zero acceleration
under isometric/isokinetic conditions. Despite equal force output, these methods are
argued and shown in practice not to produce the same training effect, because different
neural, muscular, and metabolic processes are engaged in each case. (PDF pp. 32-33,
printed pp. 21-22.)

**Why it works** — The text bases the "do not produce the same results" claim on "practical
experience from three different competitive aspects of strength training" (powerlifting,
weightlifting, bodybuilding; printed 22), not on a stated mechanism. Inference: force alone
does not specify the movement's velocity, duration, muscle action type, or motor unit
recruitment/firing pattern, all of which independently affect the training stimulus; two
efforts that reach the same peak force via different mass-acceleration combinations are
mechanically equal on that one variable but different on several others that matter
physiologically.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a reasoning check against choosing exercises
solely by "how much force does this produce," when the intended adaptation (max strength
vs. explosive power vs. hypertrophy vs. isometric endurance) requires matching the
mass-acceleration profile, not just the force magnitude, to the target quality. This
generalized application is this entry's own extension of the four loading-option
comparison (PDF pp. 32-33, printed pp. 21-22).

**When NOT to apply** — The authors state isokinetic training (option d, F = k.R)
correlates poorly with actual sporting performance despite producing meaningful
non-specific strength gains in a lab setting (PDF p. 33, printed p. 22, citing Rosentzweig
& Hinson 1972, Ostemig 1986). **Inference:** don't treat isokinetic results as a proxy for
how an athlete will perform in ballistic, free-loading sport actions; this specific
caution is this entry's own restatement of that finding's practical implication.
Inference: for hypertrophy specifically, load magnitude matters less than effort: similar
hypertrophy is reported across a wide load range when sets are taken to failure (Schoenfeld
et al. 2017, JSCR), so the "do not produce the same results" claim is more load-outcome-
specific than the text's general statement suggests.

**Example** — **Inference:** A powerlifting-style heavy squat and an Olympic-style ballistic
clean pull can both produce a similar peak force at the bar, but the clean pull's high
acceleration under a lighter relative load trains rate of force development and ballistic
coordination that the heavy, slow squat does not, and vice versa for maximal-tension
adaptation.

**Related** — [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]].
confidence: supported
=================== principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity
# The Force-Velocity Relationship, and Why Strength Doesn't Guarantee Speed

**What it is** — Hill's hyperbolic force-velocity curve: velocity of contraction is
inversely related to load; large force cannot be produced at very high velocities under
constant conditions; heavy strength training shifts the curve upward, particularly in
beginners (raising force at all velocities, called training for "strength-speed"); light,
high-velocity training shifts the curve's velocity maximum rightward (called training for
"speed-strength"). Because power = force x velocity, both shifts raise power, just at
different points on the curve. Zatsiorsky (1995) reports "there is no correlation between
maximal velocity and maximal strength" (printed 20); the ability to generate maximum
strength and to produce high speed are described as different motor abilities. Inference:
this specific claim is contested by modern data (Wisloff et al. 2004, Br J Sports Med
38:285, squat 1RM vs. 10 m sprint time, r ~0.94; Seitz et al. 2014, Sports Med, strength
gains transferring to sprint performance). (PDF pp. 30-31, printed pp. 19-20; Zatsiorsky &
Matveev 1964, Komi 1979, Zatsiorsky 1995.)

**Why it works** — The Hill curve, "although this relationship originally was derived for
isolated muscle, ... has been confirmed for actual sporting movement" (printed 19). Beyond
that author's statement, the rest is Inference: the F-V relationship reflects the
cross-bridge cycling and motor unit recruitment limits of muscle contraction, and is the
conceptual ancestor of the force-velocity profiling methods (Samozino, Morin, and others)
used in modern sprint and jump testing; the book does not itself draw that connection to
modern profiling.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** justifies programming that targets a specific region of
the force-velocity spectrum rather than assuming "more strength" automatically transfers to
speed: heavy-load, low-velocity work develops the force end; light-load, high-velocity
(including ballistic/plyometric) work develops the velocity end. **Inference:** usable as
the conceptual basis for choosing between a strength-speed or speed-strength emphasis block
for an athlete whose limiter has been identified (e.g., via jump testing or sprint
force-velocity profiling); this specific screening application is not stated in the text.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** don't treat "no correlation between max strength and
max velocity" (PDF p. 31, printed p. 20) as license to ignore strength training for a
speed-limited athlete; a certain strength floor is plausibly still necessary before
speed-specific training pays off. **Eric's baseline:** the Vermeil hierarchy of athletic
development (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill) is
repeatedly described as the department's programming "compass" (`method-baseline.md`,
"Strength and power," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.9-10,18-19`).
**Inference:** that sequencing is broadly consistent with treating a strength floor as a
prerequisite, though neither this text's cited section nor the baseline states the two
frameworks are equivalent. The text itself flags the classic hyperbolic F-V curve as not
universally accurate: research on the lumbar erector spinae shows a "yielding" drop in
force during constant-velocity eccentric stretching that the standard curve doesn't predict
(Sutarno & McGill, 1995; PDF p. 30, printed p. 19) — the model is a strong generalization,
not a universal law for every muscle group.

**Example** — **Inference:** Two athletes with equal back squat 1RM (similar max force) can have very
different unloaded sprint speeds; that gap is F-V curve position, not raw strength, and
argues for velocity-end training (sprint work, light-load ballistics) rather than more
heavy squatting to close it.

**Related** — [[principle--torque-optimization-in-lifting-technique]],
[[principle--equal-force-different-loading-methods]].

=================== principle--neuromuscular-stimulation-drives-early-strength-gains
# Strength Increase Is Initiated by Neuromuscular Stimulation, Not Muscle Size

**What it is** — "The fundamental principle of strength training... is that all strength
increase is initiated by neuromuscular stimulation." Strength is framed as a function of
how powerfully and efficiently muscle is activated by the nervous system first, with
hypertrophy as a downstream, longer-term structural consequence of a given stimulus
regime, not the driver of early gains. (PDF pp. 17-18, printed pp. 6-7.)

**Why it works** — Inference: force output can rise before cross-sectional area change
translates into more strength through improved recruitment, firing rate, and coordination
of the muscle already present. Early strength gains outpacing measurable hypertrophy is a
replicated finding in resistance training research outside this text; whether hypertrophy
itself contributes meaningfully to early strength gains, versus being purely downstream, is
an active debate (Loenneke et al. 2019 vs. Taber et al. 2019, both Sports Med), which is
why this entry is capped at `supported` rather than `proven` for the broader "not muscle
size" framing.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this principle explains early-training-block strength
gains in novice athletes that outpace any visible muscle growth. **Eric's baseline:**
Tracy Fober's "use a barbell like a chisel, not a sledgehammer" standard prioritizes
movement quality and confidence-through-competence over chasing hypertrophy or 1RM
numbers, especially early in a training cycle (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power,"
citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.21`; `week1-lecture.md p.46`).
**Inference:** that coaching standard is consistent with this principle's emphasis on
coordination before load, though the baseline material does not itself cite the
neuromuscular-primacy mechanism. **Inference:** the same logic likely explains why
detraining strength loss can outpace measurable muscle loss (neural efficiency degrading
faster than tissue), though this text does not state that extension explicitly.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors state maximal strength "depends to a great extent"
on adequate muscle cross-section (PDF p. 18, printed p. 7), so hypertrophy is not
unimportant at higher training ages. **Inference:** this principle should not be used to
justify skipping hypertrophy-phase work for athletes past the early-adaptation window,
where structural gains matter more for continued strength progress; this caution is not
stated in the text itself. The book itself also notes muscle mass "increases markedly
within a few days of functional overload," though that early hypertrophy "offers little or
no increase in strength" during the first week or so (printed 61); early gains outpacing
hypertrophy is not the same as hypertrophy being absent in that window.

**Example** — **Inference:** A freshman who has never lifted seriously often adds meaningful strength in
the first 4-6 weeks of a program with little visible size change; that gain is
predominantly neural (coordination, recruitment, reduced antagonist co-contraction), not
tissue growth.

**Related** — [[framework--functional-vs-structural-resistance-training]] (the
mechanisms by which this happens).
confidence: supported
=================== principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter
# Rate of Force (or Tension) Development Is a Separate Limiter from Maximal Force

**What it is** — Sporting performance does not depend simply on the ability to produce
maximum force, because many sporting actions happen too fast to recruit an adequate
number of muscle fibres in the available time. Rate of Force Development (RFD) / Rate of
Tension Development (RTD) — how quickly force rises, not just its ceiling — is named as an
independently important limiter, worth assessing on its own alongside maximal-force
deficits. (PDF p. 21, printed p. 10; cross-referenced to 2.2.1 for more detail.)

**Why it works** — Inference: many athletic actions (sprint ground contact, jump takeoff,
change of direction) last far less time than it takes to reach true maximal voluntary
force. An athlete can have high 1RM strength but a slow force-time curve, and still
underperform in short-duration actions, because the task ends before peak force is reached.
This distinction (peak force vs. rate of rise to a sub-maximal time point) is well
established in modern force-time curve analysis outside this text, which the text itself
does not cite.

**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** force-plate metric selection follows the
Output/Driver/Strategy/Fluffy (ODSF) framework, picking 1-2 output metrics, 1-3 driver
metrics (e.g. braking/propulsive force), and 1-3 strategy metrics (e.g. phase durations)
rather than reporting peak values alone (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and
neuromuscular monitoring," citing `hd-odsf-metrics.md`, credited to Hawkin Dynamics, not
Eric's own framework). **Inference:** this principle's force-vs-rate distinction supports
that driver-metric emphasis and argues for testing and reporting RFD-type variables
separately from 1RM or peak-force values, especially for athletes in short-ground-contact
positions; this specific link between the ODSF framework and Verkhoshansky's RFD argument
is not stated in either source.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** don't substitute a single RFD number for the full
force-time curve when the movement or time window matters (RFD at 0-50ms is a different
quality than RFD at 100-200ms); this time-window caution is this entry's own addition, not
stated in this section of the text. The authors cross-reference RFD/RTD deficits to 2.2.1
and the strength-deficit discussion to 3.2.1 (PDF p. 21, printed p. 10); Inference: this
implies the two qualities are trainable somewhat independently, though the text does not
state that implication directly.

**Example** — **Inference:** Two athletes with the same back squat 1RM can produce very different sprint
starts if one reaches a given force threshold in 100ms and the other takes 200ms; testing
and training that difference requires RFD-sensitive measures, not another max-strength
test.

**Related** — [[heuristic--strength-deficit-sets-training-method-choice]].
confidence: proven
=================== principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy
# A Short Transition (Amortization) Between Stretch and Shortening Preserves Stored Elastic Energy

**What it is** — "The lifetime of the cross-bridges between actin and myosin strands is
limited, varying from 15 to 120 milliseconds" (printed 47, no citation given in the text
for this figure). For stored elastic energy from a stretch to be used in the following
concentric contraction, the transition period between the end of the eccentric (stretch)
phase and the start of the concentric (shortening) phase must be brief; a longer delay lets
cross-bridges detach ("a more prolonged delay will allow fewer cross-bridges to remain
attached after the stretch," Edman et al., 1978, printed 45) and the elastic potential
dissipates as slippage rather than being used for work. A greater velocity of stretch
during the eccentric phase also increases elastic energy storage (Rack & Westbury, 1974,
printed 45). Much of the extra positive work seen in rapid eccentric-concentric
(plyometric) actions is attributed to this stored elastic energy plus a separate

=================== principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter
# Rate of Force (or Tension) Development Is a Separate Limiter from Maximal Force

**What it is** — Sporting performance does not depend simply on the ability to produce
maximum force, because many sporting actions happen too fast to recruit an adequate
number of muscle fibres in the available time. Rate of Force Development (RFD) / Rate of
Tension Development (RTD) — how quickly force rises, not just its ceiling — is named as an
independently important limiter, worth assessing on its own alongside maximal-force
deficits. (PDF p. 21, printed p. 10; cross-referenced to 2.2.1 for more detail.)

**Why it works** — Inference: many athletic actions (sprint ground contact, jump takeoff,
change of direction) last far less time than it takes to reach true maximal voluntary
force. An athlete can have high 1RM strength but a slow force-time curve, and still
underperform in short-duration actions, because the task ends before peak force is reached.
This distinction (peak force vs. rate of rise to a sub-maximal time point) is well
established in modern force-time curve analysis outside this text, which the text itself
does not cite.

**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** force-plate metric selection follows the
Output/Driver/Strategy/Fluffy (ODSF) framework, picking 1-2 output metrics, 1-3 driver
metrics (e.g. braking/propulsive force), and 1-3 strategy metrics (e.g. phase durations)
rather than reporting peak values alone (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and
neuromuscular monitoring," citing `hd-odsf-metrics.md`, credited to Hawkin Dynamics, not
Eric's own framework). **Inference:** this principle's force-vs-rate distinction supports
that driver-metric emphasis and argues for testing and reporting RFD-type variables
separately from 1RM or peak-force values, especially for athletes in short-ground-contact
positions; this specific link between the ODSF framework and Verkhoshansky's RFD argument
is not stated in either source.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** don't substitute a single RFD number for the full
force-time curve when the movement or time window matters (RFD at 0-50ms is a different
quality than RFD at 100-200ms); this time-window caution is this entry's own addition, not
stated in this section of the text. The authors cross-reference RFD/RTD deficits to 2.2.1
and the strength-deficit discussion to 3.2.1 (PDF p. 21, printed p. 10); Inference: this
implies the two qualities are trainable somewhat independently, though the text does not
state that implication directly.

**Example** — **Inference:** Two athletes with the same back squat 1RM can produce very different sprint
starts if one reaches a given force threshold in 100ms and the other takes 200ms; testing
and training that difference requires RFD-sensitive measures, not another max-strength
test.

=================== claim--collagen-loading-curve-and-injury-risk
# Collagenous Tissue's Four-Region Loading Curve, and Why Loading Rate Changes What Fails First

**What it is** — Collagenous tissue (e.g. the ACL, studied by Frankel & Nordin 1980)
loaded to failure shows four regions: Region I, the "toe region," where the crimped
tissue straightens with little force and mild stretching here produces no long-term
flexibility change; Region II, a near-linear region where fibres are fully uncrimped and
parallel; Region III, where sequential microfailure of overstretched fibres begins; Region
IV, complete failure. Loading rate changes the outcome: increasing loading rate roughly
fourfold raised knee ligament failure load by almost 50% (Kennedy et al., 1976), and which
structure fails first flips with rate — at slow loading rates the ligament's bony
insertion is the weakest link, while at fast loading rates the ligament itself is the
weakest link (bone's strength rises faster with rate than the ligament's). Healthy tendon's
tensile strength can be more than twice that of its associated muscle, which is why
ruptures are more common in muscle than tendon. (PDF pp. 54-56, printed pp. 43-45.)

**Why it works** — Collagen is viscoelastic: it behaves more elastically under rapid
loading and more plastically (creeping, deforming) under slow, sustained loading, so both
the loading speed and the tissue's own rate-dependent stiffness change determine where in
the body an excessive load actually causes failure.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** relevant background for understanding why static
stretching held gently (Region I) does not meaningfully change tissue length or
flexibility over time, and why ballistic or rapid loading, once past Region II, carries
real microfailure risk; also relevant context for why the pattern of injury (bone
avulsion vs. mid-ligament tear vs. muscle strain) can differ by the speed of the loading
event, which matters for how Athletic Medicine and Applied Performance jointly interpret
an injury mechanism.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is basic tissue mechanics from cited
1970s-1980s cadaveric/animal ligament research, not a live-tissue, in-vivo human athlete
dataset; do not use the specific numbers (50% failure-load increase, the fourfold rate
figure) as applicable outside the original knee-ligament loading-rate study (Kennedy 1976,
printed 44); only the strain curve (Fig 1.21) is specifically ACL.
This is background science, not a clinical decision rule, and should not substitute for
Athletic Medicine's own injury assessment framework.

**Example** — **Inference:** a sudden high-rate valgus load to the knee is more likely to
produce mid-ligament ACL failure, while a slower, sustained load is more likely to fail at
the bony insertion first; this pattern helps explain, but does not replace, imaging and
clinical exam in determining actual injury location.

**Related** — [[claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates]],
[[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]].

# Soviet Sport-School Guideline Ages by Sport (Start, Specialize, Peak)

**What it is** — A per-sport table (Table 1.2) of recommended ages to begin a sport,
begin specialization, and expect high performance, drawn from the Soviet sports-school
system. Examples: basketball 7-8 / 10-12 / 20-25; gymnastics (women) 4-5 / 10-11 / 14-18;
gymnastics (men) 5-6 / 12-14 / 18-24; swimming 3-7 / 10-12 / 16-18; track-and-field 6-7 /
13-14 / 18-23; weightlifting 10-11 / 17-18 / 21-28; wrestling 10-11 / 15-16 / 24-28 (17
sports listed in total). Early, intense specialization is explicitly discouraged in
strength and endurance sports for children; the average age of Soviet Olympians in the
era cited was about 24, with fewer than 10% under age 20. (PDF pp. 35-36, printed pp.
24-25.)

**Why it works** — **Inference:** the likely underlying rationale matches this library's
existing long-term athletic development material — early specialization in
strength/endurance sports produces faster short-term progress but a lower ultimate ceiling

# Collagenous Tissue's Four-Region Loading Curve, and Why Loading Rate Changes What Fails First

**What it is** — Collagenous tissue (e.g. the ACL, studied by Frankel & Nordin 1980)
loaded to failure shows four regions: Region I, the "toe region," where the crimped
tissue straightens with little force and mild stretching here produces no long-term
flexibility change; Region II, a near-linear region where fibres are fully uncrimped and
parallel; Region III, where sequential microfailure of overstretched fibres begins; Region
IV, complete failure. Loading rate changes the outcome: increasing loading rate roughly
fourfold raised knee ligament failure load by almost 50% (Kennedy et al., 1976), and which
structure fails first flips with rate — at slow loading rates the ligament's bony
insertion is the weakest link, while at fast loading rates the ligament itself is the
weakest link (bone's strength rises faster with rate than the ligament's). Healthy tendon's
tensile strength can be more than twice that of its associated muscle, which is why
ruptures are more common in muscle than tendon. (PDF pp. 54-56, printed pp. 43-45.)

**Why it works** — Collagen is viscoelastic: it behaves more elastically under rapid
loading and more plastically (creeping, deforming) under slow, sustained loading, so both
the loading speed and the tissue's own rate-dependent stiffness change determine where in
the body an excessive load actually causes failure.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** relevant background for understanding why static
stretching held gently (Region I) does not meaningfully change tissue length or
flexibility over time, and why ballistic or rapid loading, once past Region II, carries
real microfailure risk; also relevant context for why the pattern of injury (bone
avulsion vs. mid-ligament tear vs. muscle strain) can differ by the speed of the loading
event, which matters for how Athletic Medicine and Applied Performance jointly interpret
an injury mechanism.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is basic tissue mechanics from cited
1970s-1980s cadaveric/animal ligament research, not a live-tissue, in-vivo human athlete
dataset; do not use the specific numbers (50% failure-load increase, the fourfold rate
figure) as applicable outside the original knee-ligament loading-rate study (Kennedy 1976,
printed 44); only the strain curve (Fig 1.21) is specifically ACL.
This is background science, not a clinical decision rule, and should not substitute for
Athletic Medicine's own injury assessment framework.

**Example** — **Inference:** a sudden high-rate valgus load to the knee is more likely to
produce mid-ligament ACL failure, while a slower, sustained load is more likely to fail at
the bony insertion first; this pattern helps explain, but does not replace, imaging and
clinical exam in determining actual injury location.

[[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]].

=================== framework--precise-muscle-action-terminology
# Precise Muscle-Action Terminology: Why "Isotonic" and "Isokinetic" Are Usually Wrong

**What it is** — The authors argue most everyday strength-training terms are
technically imprecise. Concentric: proximal and distal muscle attachments move toward one
another. Eccentric: they move apart (not literally a "contraction," despite the common
name — the muscle is returning toward resting length under load). Isometric: attachments
don't move relative to each other (joint angle constant); more accurately called "static."
"Isotonic" (constant tension) is argued to be almost never actually true during real joint
movement, since tension changes with acceleration, deceleration, and reflex activation
throughout a range; European and Russian scientists prefer "auxotonic" (changing tension
and length) or "allodynamic" instead. "Isokinetic" (constant velocity) is also argued to
be physically impossible over a full range, since starting from and returning to rest
requires acceleration; isokinetic devices are more accurately "quasi-isokinetic," and
isokinetic-machine torque output is typically much lower than isometric torque at the same
joint angle. "Quasi-isometric" action is defined separately: the slow, near-static muscle
action seen in heavy, near-maximal resistance training performed anywhere across a joint's
range (not fixed at one angle like true isometrics), relevant to maximal strength,
hypertrophy, and active flexibility training rather than power or speed. (PDF pp. 60-64,
printed pp. 49-53.)

**Why it works** — Real joint movement always involves changing acceleration
(Newton's laws), so any term implying a truly constant mechanical variable throughout a
full range is describing an idealization, not the actual muscle physics; the more precise
terms track what is actually held constant and where.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** relevant when interpreting or reporting isokinetic
dynamometer data (if used by Athletic Medicine or research collaborators): understand that
the constant-velocity claim applies only to the device's controlled range, not to the
underlying muscle action, and that isokinetic torque values are not directly comparable to
isometric (e.g. IMTP) values at the same joint angle. Also useful coaching-language
precision: heavy squat/bench-style lifting performed slowly is "quasi-isometric," a
distinct quality from true fixed-angle isometrics like the IMTP.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a terminology-precision argument, not a
claim that isokinetic or isotonic training methods are ineffective; the critique is about
what the words accurately describe, not about training value. Don't over-correct common
usage in casual coaching communication where the imprecise terms are well understood by
convention.

**Example** — **Inference:** describing an IMTP as "isometric" (fixed joint angle) versus
a slow, heavy back squat as "quasi-isometric" (near-static but occurring across a range)
keeps clear which type of force-plate or barbell data is actually comparable to which.

**Related** — [[principle--triphasic-nature-of-muscle-action]].

=================== framework--work-capacity-fitness-preparedness
# Work Capacity, Fitness, and Preparedness Are Three Different Things

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (citing Zatsiorsky) defines three related but distinct
terms. Work capacity is the general ability of the body to produce work of different
intensity and duration using its energy systems. Fitness is the specific ability to use
that work capacity to execute a given task efficiently and safely; it is a slow-changing
state that does not vary meaningfully over a period of days. Preparedness is not stable:
it is the resultant, at any given instant, of the interaction between the slow-changing
fitness component and the fast-changing, opposing effect of exercise-induced fatigue.
"Instantaneous preparedness" can be pushed down by transient factors (mental state,
sickness, fatigue, sleepiness) without any change in underlying fitness. (PDF pp. 43-44,

# All Dynamic Movement Is Triphasic: Isometric, Then Concentric/Eccentric, Then Isometric Again

**What it is** — Classifying muscle action as simply "static" (isometric) or "dynamic"
(concentric/eccentric) is described as an oversimplification. Every dynamic action must
begin from an isometric phase (the muscle must first develop enough tension to
counterbalance the load before any movement starts: concentric if tension exceeds the
load, eccentric if it doesn't), and every movement ends in another isometric phase before
reversing or stopping, because Newton's laws require the system to momentarily come to
rest at a direction change. In ballistic/ fast movement, the transition isometric phase is
very brief; in slow maximal efforts (e.g. a powerlifting squat or bench), it can be much
longer. The brief isometric phase in a plyometric movement is specifically termed
"explosive isometric" action and is central to speed-strength training and movements like
the weightlifting jerk, shot put, and high jump. Movement termination/reversal can also
involve any combination of agonist eccentric or isometric action, antagonist concentric or
isometric action, stabilizer action at the joint or nearby joints, and passive connective-
tissue damping — not simply "antagonist opposes agonist" as popular descriptions suggest.
(PDF pp. 65-66, printed pp. 54-55.)

have zero velocity at the instant it reverses direction) combined with the physiological
fact that muscle tension must build before it can move a load; the "explosive isometric"
phase is the same brief coupling window discussed in

whole-joint-action perspective rather than the cross-bridge perspective.

niche quality but a phase present in every dynamic lift and sprint/jump action, which

relevant to dynamic performance, not a side quality. Also a caution for kinesiology

# Precise Muscle-Action Terminology: Why "Isotonic" and "Isokinetic" Are Usually Wrong

**What it is** — The authors argue most everyday strength-training terms are
technically imprecise. Concentric: proximal and distal muscle attachments move toward one
another. Eccentric: they move apart (not literally a "contraction," despite the common
name — the muscle is returning toward resting length under load). Isometric: attachments
don't move relative to each other (joint angle constant); more accurately called "static."
"Isotonic" (constant tension) is argued to be almost never actually true during real joint
movement, since tension changes with acceleration, deceleration, and reflex activation
throughout a range; European and Russian scientists prefer "auxotonic" (changing tension
and length) or "allodynamic" instead. "Isokinetic" (constant velocity) is also argued to
be physically impossible over a full range, since starting from and returning to rest
requires acceleration; isokinetic devices are more accurately "quasi-isokinetic," and
isokinetic-machine torque output is typically much lower than isometric torque at the same
joint angle. "Quasi-isometric" action is defined separately: the slow, near-static muscle
action seen in heavy, near-maximal resistance training performed anywhere across a joint's
range (not fixed at one angle like true isometrics), relevant to maximal strength,
hypertrophy, and active flexibility training rather than power or speed. (PDF pp. 60-64,
printed pp. 49-53.)

**Why it works** — Real joint movement always involves changing acceleration
(Newton's laws), so any term implying a truly constant mechanical variable throughout a
full range is describing an idealization, not the actual muscle physics; the more precise
terms track what is actually held constant and where.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** relevant when interpreting or reporting isokinetic
dynamometer data (if used by Athletic Medicine or research collaborators): understand that
the constant-velocity claim applies only to the device's controlled range, not to the
underlying muscle action, and that isokinetic torque values are not directly comparable to
isometric (e.g. IMTP) values at the same joint angle. Also useful coaching-language
precision: heavy squat/bench-style lifting performed slowly is "quasi-isometric," a
distinct quality from true fixed-angle isometrics like the IMTP.

claim that isokinetic or isotonic training methods are ineffective; the critique is about

convention.

strength (voluntary effort) produced in a given action and absolute strength (involuntary effort) o f which the
athlete is capable in that same action. This deficit may be defined under static or dynamic conditions, with the
deficit depending on the rate at which force has to be developed in a given joint action. In the laboratory
situation, absolute strength may be estimated by subjecting the muscles concerned to the maximum electrical
stimulation which can be tolerated.

    Since the maximum force which may be exerted depends on the load, one may define a strength deficit at
different loads, according to the force-time curve shown in Figure 3.3. Zatsiorsky (1995) defines an explosive
strength deficit as the difference between the maximum force produced under any condition and what he terms the
maximum maximorum, Fmm (the maximum o f all maxima).

    Strength deficit reflects the percentage o f maximal strength potential which is not used during a given motor
task, but its accurate measurement is seldom performed in practice, because determination o f maximum contractile
strength by electrical stimulation is a difficult and potentially harmful task, and even if this were not the case,
most sporting actions involve many muscles and joints, so that measurements o f deficits for separate muscle
groups would not necessarily relate to performance deficits in complex tasks.

    The closest one can approach involuntary recruitment o f as many muscle fibres in a given task is to force the
body to react by reflex action to a suddenly imposed load. Thus, in a jum ping or pulling activity, an approximate
measure of strength deficit may be made by comparing the vertical jum p achieved from a static start with knees
flexed with a vertical jum p preceded by a sudden dip. If there is a small difference between the two jum ps, this
suggests that training focuses more on nervous stimulation via the use o f `shock' and ballistic methods such as

                                                                       9

                                                                  SUPERTRAINING

plyomctrics. If the deficit is large, then strength and hypertrophy training with 5RM to 8RM (8 repetition
maximum) loads using methods such as CAT (Compensatory Activation Training) is more suitable.

     In general, if the strength deficit is large for a given muscle group, an increase in speed-strcngth may be
produced by maximal or near-maximal neuromuscular stimulation (e.g. via weightlifting or plyometric methods).
If the strength deficit is small, hypertrophy must be induced by submaximal loading methods as commonly used
in bodybuilding, followed by maximal efforts against heavy loads.

     Verkhoshansky has shown that the strength deficit increases as the external resistance and the time o f motion
decrease (see 3.2.1), indicating that training to increase maximum or absolute strength becomes more important as
the time available for a movement becomes longer. Conversely, training to increase rapidity o f movement (i.e.
nervous system conditioning) becomes more important as the external load decreases. His work implies that
estimation o f explosive strength deficit is also more important in devising strength training regimes for athletes
whose events do not allow them sufficient time to produce maximum force, in other words, for actions such as
running, jum ping and throwing. Chapter 3.2.1 gives further essential information on his research into the strength
deficit and its relevance to training to increase power and explosive strength.

     Before attempting to estimate strength deficit it is important to appreciate that sporting performance does
not depend simply on the ability to produce maximum force, since many sporting actions take place so rapidly that
it is im possible to recruit an adequate num ber o f muscle fibres. Presuming that technical skill is adequate,
performance may also be limited by the inability to produce the optimal level o f strength at any given instant. In
other words. Rate o f Force Development (RFD) or Rate o f Tension Development (RTD) in the muscles are other
factors which are vital to sporting prowess. Thus, it can be highly relevant to estimate deficits in maximalforce
production as well as in the Rate o f Force Production (2.2.1).

     Identification o f the strength deficit for the most important muscle groups o f an athlete enables the coach to
design the specific type o f strength training more accurately than relying on the more conventional approach of
fairly arbitrarily prescribing a certain number o f sets and repetitions o f several exercises with a given load.
Development o f the necessary type o f sport specific fitness entails far more than this: the training programme
must also pay careful attention to many other factors including the method o f executing each exercise and the
manner in which force is displayed relative to time and space (other factors are listed in the following section).

     As stated earlier, i f the strength deficit is large for a given muscle group, an increase in speed-strength may be
produced by maximal or near-maximal neuromuscular stimulation (e.g. via weightlifting or plyometric methods).
I f the strength deficit is small, hypertrophy must be induced by sub-maximal loading methods as commonly used
in bodybuilding (see Table 1.1 and Ch 7), followed by maximal efforts against heavy loads. A more enduring type
o f strength fitness results from a well-sequenced combination o f functional and structural resistance training.
However, it is important to monitor regularly any change in relative strength to ascertain if increased hypertrophy

content.content:
SUPERTRAINING

Training programmes based entirely on these variables, however, are seriously incomplete and limited in their
long-term effectiveness, especially as a form o f supplementary training for other sports. Factors such as the
following must also be taken into consideration:

      � the type o f strength fitness required
      � the type o f muscle contraction involved (isometric, concentric, eccentric)
      � the speed o f movement over different phases o f movement
      � the acceleration at critical points in the movement
      � the rest intervals between repetitions, sets and workouts
      � active versus passive rest/recuperation intervals
      � the sequence o f exercises
      � the relative strength o f agonists and antagonists, stabilisers and movers
      � the development o f optimal static and dynamic range o f movement
      � the strength deficit o f given muscle groups
      � the training history o f the individual
      � the injury history o f the individual
      � the level o f sports proficiency o f the individual.

The last-mentioned factor is o f exceptional importance, because the advanced athlete responds to a given training
regime very differently from a novice. For instance, the exact sequencing o f strength, strcngth-speed and
hypertrophy means in a workout or microcycle is o f little consequence during the first weeks or months o f a
beginner's training, but is very important to a more experienced athlete. Moreover, loads as small as 40% o f 1RM
can significantly enhance the strength o f a beginner, but have no strengthening effect on an elite athlete.

1.1.2 F a c to rs L im itin g S tre n g th P ro d u ctio n

The production o f strength in the short and long term depends on the following main factors:

� Trainability              � Pain and Fear o f Pain
� Neuromuscular Efficiency  � Injury and Fear o f Injury
� Biomechanical Efficiency  � Fatigue
� Psychological Factors

T rain ab ility This refers to the potential to develop strength in response to a specific training regime and
depends largely on genetic factors and pre-training status. Genetic factors determine the potential for
hypertrophy, the leverage characteristics about each joint, the distribution o f fast and slow twitch fibres in the
different muscle groups, and metabolic efficiency. The pre-training status refers to the level o f special fitness
possessed by an individual before formal training begins. Physical loading imposed by work, play and casual
sport has a pronounced effect on one's ability to gain strength, with the greatest relative increases being possible
among untrained individuals and the smallest among elite athletes. Individual response to training at a given level
o f special fitness, however, is governed largely by one's genetic predisposition to increase hypertrophy, strength
and power easily. Moreover, during long-term training, the blood serum levels o f biologically active unbound
testosterone may also be o f importance for trainability (Hakkinen, 1985).

                                                                  SUPERTRAINING

which records both the objective loading and the subjective rating offers a more thorough means o f adjusting one's
training programme and minimising the likelihood o f overtraining and overtraining injury.

       In applying any form o f RPE, it should be noted that the scale is not linear, but has been found to increase
exponentially (Banister, 1979). In other words, a rating o f 6 docs not mean that the effort is perceived as twice
that at a rating o f 3. Moreover, if a load is doubled, the perceived rating does not double.

In ju ry an d F e a r o f In ju ry It requires no sophisticated analysis to confirm that acute or chronic injury may
make it impossible for one to produce maximal strength. In particular, reflex inhibition o f contraction is a well-
known phenomenon which produces muscle weakness when a joint is damaged (Stokes & Young, 1984). For
example, it is impossible to generate maximal squatting strength if one is suffering from knee joint deterioration
such as chondromalacia patellae or any other form o f peripatellar damage. The importance o f prescribing efficient
and safe training to develop strength then becomes obvious, as does the use o f appropriate rehabilitation regimens
to restore the injured athlete to top-level competition. Fear o f injury or pain must be recognised as a major
inhibitory factor in the production o f strength or any other motor qualities, for that matter. It is often largely
unimportant if medical assessment pronounces rehabilitation to be complete; return to top level performance will
occur only i f the athlete perceives rehabilitation to be complete and the fear o f pain or re-injury to be minimal.

Fatigue Fatigue determines one's ability to sustain a specific type o f effort, ranging from the supreme
cardiovascular demands o f ultra-marathon races to the short-term maximal strength bouts o f weightlifters and
powerlifters. Rapid fatigue is induced by the maximal and near-maximal efforts associated with strength sports
(such as weightlifting and powerlifting) and slow fatigue with sports which involve low intensities o f strength
production (such as distance running and cycling).

       Endurance may be defined as the ability to resist fatigue, static endurance the ability to sustain isometric
activity and dynamic endurance the ability to sustain dynamic muscle contraction. It should be noted that
dynamic endurance for the different modes o f muscle action (auxotonic, isotonic or isokinetic) is not the same, nor
is endurance at different velocities o f motion the same. This is one reason why fitness qualities such as specd-
endurance, static strength-endurance, dynamic strength-endurance and speed-strength endurance are defined.

      A distinction is made between centralfatigue and peripheralfatigue, where the former is associated with the
central nervous system, i.e. factors outside the muscular system, and the latter refers to fatigue processes in the
peripheral nervous system and the neuromuscular system. Central fatigue relates to decreased motivation,
impaired transmission o f spinal nerve impulses and impaired recruitment o f spinal motor neurons (Bigland*
Ritchie & Woods, 1984).

      Fatigue at muscle cell level may affect one or more of the many excitation-contraction processes which begin
with depolarisation o f the muscle cell at the neuromuscular junction and end with the mechanical pow er stroke,
the final action involved in actin-myosin interaction and force generation. Disturbance at any stage o f this chain of
processes will low er the capability o f a muscle cell o f realising its maximum force potential. The primary
peripheral sites which have been implicated in muscle cell fatigue include the motor end-plate, the sarcolemma, the
T tubules, the sarcoplasmic reticulum, regulatory proteins and contractile proteins (Green, 1988).

       Some scientists have also suggested a significant role for ammonia in the fatigue process. Exercise-induced
hyperammonemia refers to increased ammonia accumulation during exercise (Banister & Cameron, 1990).
Ammonia is a ubiquitous metabolic byproduct which exerts multiple effects on physiological and biochemical
systems. Depending on the intensity and duration o f exercise, muscle ammonia may rise sufficiently to leak from
muscle to blood, and thereby travel to other organs. The direction of movement o f ammonia or the ammonium ion
is dependent on concentration and pH gradients between tissues. Thus, ammonia can also cross the blood-brain
barrier, although the rate o f diffusion o f ammonia from blood to brain during exercise is unknown. Consequently,
exhaustive exercise may induce a state o f acute ammonia toxicity which, although transient and reversible relative
to disease states, may be severe enough in critical regions o f the CNS to hinder further coordinated activity.

       Peripheral fatigue has been subdivided further into lowfrequencyfatigue and high frequency fatigue, with the
distinction being made on the basis o f the frequency at which fatigue occurs in response to electrical stimulation
o f the muscles (Edwards, 1981). If electrical stimulation is applied to a muscle directly after contraction,
impairment in force production at low frequency (less than 20 Hz) has been called low frequency fatigue by
 Edwards. If the force decrement is detected at frequencies greater than 50 Hz, this is known as high frequency
fatigue (Fig 1.5).

SUPERTRAINING

Mechanical-Metabolic  Electromechanical

Figure 13 Classification o f the different types o f fatigue

     Low frequency (LF) fatigue occurs early in exercise, without regard to the characteristics o f muscle
contraction, and exhibits a prolonged recovery period persisting for as long as 48 hours. It has been attributed to
failure in excitation coupling due to depressed release o f calcium ions (Edwards, 1981). It does not necessarily
affect force output at high frequency, because the high excitation frequency may compensate for the impaired
release and maximally activate the muscle fibre. Interestingly, it has been found that variable-frequency trains of
impulses offset low frequency fatigue in skeletal muscle, so it appears as if such variability may exploit the catch
like property o f skeletal muscle to augment force in fatigued skeletal muscle (Russ & Binder-Macleod, 1999).

     It has also been shown that fatigue slows the dissociation o f force-generating myosin cross bridges, since
calcium ion uptake, the calcium ion-ATPase activity o f the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) and the rates o f SR
calcium ion release are depressed in fatigued muscles (Williams et al, 1998). Moreover, during fatigue, the
contractile apparatus and SR undergo intrinsic functional alterations, which probably results in altered force
production and energy consumption by the intact muscle.

     With reference to short-term maximal contractions, the reduction in neuromuscular transmission rates may be
a result of a reduction in central drive rather than peripheral electrical failure (Bigland-Ritchie & Woods, 1984).
This has been suggested because the reduction in firing rate may be beneficial in avoiding electrical failure and
facilitating maximal mechanical response from the muscle. Intensive activation o f the central nervous system
through the use o f training with maximal weights, maximal power or plyometrics requires a recovery period o f at
least 48 hours or more, if restoration means are not employed. Interestingly, the rapid force recovery following
eccentric exercise is mediated at least in part by neural factors, a recovery process which may occur
independently o f cell disruption (Hortobdgyi et al, 1998).

     If we wish to understand the neural factors which contribute to fatigue, it is incorrect to state that fatigue
occurs only when a task can no longer be performed. (Gandevia, 1998). Changes in muscle afferent feedback,
motor neuronal discharge, motor cortical output, and perceived effort all develop well before an activity reaches
the physiological endurance limit o f skeletal muscle. During sustained maximal contractions, it has been found that
the discharge of motor neurones commonly declines to below the level required to produce maximal force from the
muscles, whose contractile speed usually is slowed, as a consequence. Thus, some 'central' fatigue develops.
Recent findings using electrostimuiation across the skull have revealed that the motor cortex is one site at which
suboptimal output develops during human muscle fatigue.

     The sequence o f recruitment o f the different muscle fibres is determined largely by the intensity and duration
of loading, with the low-threshold, slow-twitch, high-endurance fibres being recruited first while the intensity o f
stimulation is low, and the fast twitch, low-endurance fibres being successively recruited as the intensity of
activation increases (see Fig 1.21).

     Other studies have revealed that changes in both recruitment pattern and increased firing frequency occur in
an attempt to delay the onset o f fatigue (M aton, 1981). However, different muscles may utilise different
strategies to cope with fatigue, because the significance o f recruitment pattern and firing frequency varies between
muscles when generating isometric strength (Deluca, 1985).

     The decrease in bloodflo w to the muscles with increasing intensity o f muscle contraction also has a major
effect on local muscular endurance. The free supply o f oxygen to the muscles by the capillaries takes place only
for loads eliciting less than 15% o f maximal muscle tension. At greater levels o f tension, blood flow is
progressively more impeded by the compression of the blood vessels by the contracting muscles, until it ceases
completely when a muscle generates more than about 50% of its maximum isometric strength. At this stage the
muscle must rely on 'anaerobic' processes to meet its energy needs. If the dynam ic activity at this level o f

1.16.1 The G eneral A daptation S yndrom e

Selye's theory postulates that all anim als exposed to periods o f stress undergo three phases o f the GAS: initial
alarm, resistance and exhaustion. The energy for resistance or adaptation comes from the readily available
superficial adaptation energy source or the emergency deep adaptation energy source, depending on the level o f
exhaustion or depletion o f energy at any instant. In Russian texts, the former energy source is referred to as the
 Current Adaptation Reserves (CAR), a term which is used extensively in later sections o f this text. The capacity
 ofthese reserves is not fixed, but alters in response to the demands placed on them by stresses such as training.
 The importance o f this will become clear when the concept o f supercompensation and its applications in
---
restoration and transition periods between training sessions and not during the heavy loading phases.

      It has also been deduced that adaptive processes apparently do not just constrain bodily processes to always
produce the same, predetermined maximal level o f resistance. It has been hypothesised that they cause the body
to over-adapt, or supercompensate, to a somewhat higher level, in physiological anticipation o f repeated exposure
to the same stressor (Fig 1.39).

      This supercompensation is associated with an increase in the capacity o f the Current Adaptation Reserves
(CAR) and forms the foundation for all methods o f programming training (Ch 6). At the nutritional level, the
well-known method o f increasing bodily stores o f glycogen with significantly increased intake o f carbohydrates
after an exhausting stage o f aerobic training may be termed 'glycogen supercompensation'. Unlike the process of
fitness improvement, successive periods o f'carb o loading* do not produce progressively increased storage of
glycogen. It should also be noted that enhanced perform ance is not sim ply the result o f increased stores of
bioenergetic substances, but also o f structural changes in muscle and other tissues, as well as enhanced efficiency
and rates o f bioenergetic and neuromuscular processing (see 1.12). This is a major reason why Russian scientists
prefer to use the term adaptive reconstruction to describe the body's response to physical training.

F ig u re U 9 Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome model. The Deep Adaptation Energy is often referred to as the Current Adaptation
Reserves (CAR) by Russian authors.

Despite these shortcomings, this theory o f supercompensation had a profound impact on sports training, since it
could readily be related to the system o f carefully planned cyclical conditioning known as periodisation (Ch 6). In
brief, periodisation involves organising all components o f training (such as strength, strength-speed, cardiovascular
endurance and strength-endurance) into carefully sequenced phases (micro-, meso- and macro-cycles) of low,
medium and high intensity and volume, and regular recuperation to enable the athlete to reach specific
performance goals in given competitions over a prolonged period.
---
                                                              SUPERTRAINING

Adaptive R eco n str u c tio n v ersu s S u p ercom p en sation

As emphasized earlier, it is preferable to use a term such as adaptive reconstruction, rather than
supcrcompensation when referring to adaptation to training loads by the body. Thus, although the energy
systems or adaptation reserves would appear to have superadapted, supercompensated or overcompensated in
magnitude, there are trophic and many other changes elicited by training which are not directly related to changes
insize of energy stores. Training induced changes in muscle tissue (1.12 and 1.13) and connective tissue (1.7.2)
suchas increased tissue hypertrophy, altered muscle fibre characteristics, intensified protein synthesis, stimulated
enzyme activity, activation o f the genetic apparatus o f muscle cells and increased rate o f energy release have
alreadybeen discussed. More o f these changes will be examined in greater detail in the following section to enable
ustopresent other models o f training later in this book.

1.16.2 The B io ch em istry o f A daptation in Sport

1.16.1 The G eneral A daptation S yndrom e

Selye's theory postulates that all anim als exposed to periods o f stress undergo three phases o f the GAS: initial
alarm, resistance and exhaustion. The energy for resistance or adaptation comes from the readily available
superficial adaptation energy source or the emergency deep adaptation energy source, depending on the level o f
exhaustion or depletion o f energy at any instant. In Russian texts, the former energy source is referred to as the
 Current Adaptation Reserves (CAR), a term which is used extensively in later sections o f this text. The capacity
 ofthese reserves is not fixed, but alters in response to the demands placed on them by stresses such as training.
 The importance o f this will become clear when the concept o f supercompensation and its applications in
---
restoration and transition periods between training sessions and not during the heavy loading phases.

      It has also been deduced that adaptive processes apparently do not just constrain bodily processes to always
produce the same, predetermined maximal level o f resistance. It has been hypothesised that they cause the body
to over-adapt, or supercompensate, to a somewhat higher level, in physiological anticipation o f repeated exposure
to the same stressor (Fig 1.39).

      This supercompensation is associated with an increase in the capacity o f the Current Adaptation Reserves
(CAR) and forms the foundation for all methods o f programming training (Ch 6). At the nutritional level, the
well-known method o f increasing bodily stores o f glycogen with significantly increased intake o f carbohydrates
after an exhausting stage o f aerobic training may be termed 'glycogen supercompensation'. Unlike the process of
fitness improvement, successive periods o f'carb o loading* do not produce progressively increased storage of
glycogen. It should also be noted that enhanced perform ance is not sim ply the result o f increased stores of
bioenergetic substances, but also o f structural changes in muscle and other tissues, as well as enhanced efficiency
and rates o f bioenergetic and neuromuscular processing (see 1.12). This is a major reason why Russian scientists
prefer to use the term adaptive reconstruction to describe the body's response to physical training.

F ig u re U 9 Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome model. The Deep Adaptation Energy is often referred to as the Current Adaptation
Reserves (CAR) by Russian authors.

Despite these shortcomings, this theory o f supercompensation had a profound impact on sports training, since it
could readily be related to the system o f carefully planned cyclical conditioning known as periodisation (Ch 6). In
brief, periodisation involves organising all components o f training (such as strength, strength-speed, cardiovascular
endurance and strength-endurance) into carefully sequenced phases (micro-, meso- and macro-cycles) of low,
medium and high intensity and volume, and regular recuperation to enable the athlete to reach specific
performance goals in given competitions over a prolonged period.

magnitude, there are trophic and many other changes elicited by training which are not directly related to changes
insize of energy stores. Training induced changes in muscle tissue (1.12 and 1.13) and connective tissue (1.7.2)
suchas increased tissue hypertrophy, altered muscle fibre characteristics, intensified protein synthesis, stimulated
enzyme activity, activation o f the genetic apparatus o f muscle cells and increased rate o f energy release have
alreadybeen discussed. More o f these changes will be examined in greater detail in the following section to enable
ustopresent other models o f training later in this book.

    Although the supercompensation model has been popular for many years among scientists and coaches, its
theoretical foundation has not been comprehensively studied or proved. The depletion o f glycogen after specific
types of training and a carbohydrate loading process leading to increased glycogen storage in the body have both
been experimentally measured, but have not been observed to occur on an ongoing basis from workout to
workout, thereby leading to long-term supercompensation o f glycogen. On the contrary, ATP levels have never

                                                       87
 ---
                                                                   SUPERTRAINING
been shown to deplete significantly, even after very strenuous exercise. No supercom pensation has yet been
observed to occur among any o f the other biochemicals involved in the various bioenergctic processes in the body.
Moreover, return to their initial levels by each o f these substances after changes have been elicited by physical
stress takes a different period o f time, so the timing o f subsequent loads to stim ulate the appropriate type of
supercompcnsation remains indeterminate.


                                                                   SUPERTRAINING

T he Sequence of Biochem ical Changes during Training

The many biochemical changes that take place in the body during and after training (as well as overtraining) do not
occur simultaneously. A definite sequence in the biochemical adaptation to training is discerned (Platonov, 1988).
First, the potential for oxidative resynthesis o f ATP and the level of glycogen increase. Next there is an increase in
the level o f structural protein in the muscles (myosin) and in the intensity o f non-oxidative ATP resynthesis
(glycolysis), following which the level o f CP rises.

      In overtraining the typical changes o f biochemical adaptation acquired through training are gradually lost and
work capacity decreases. The biochemical indices during overtraining change in an order that is the reverse of the
order seen during training. Naturally, the dynamics o f developing and losing the biochemical changes of
adaptation depend on the characteristics o f the previous training. In general, the longer the training period, the
more thorough is the reorganisation by the adaptation mechanisms and the longer the accompanying biochemical
changes last in the body after cessation o f training, especially regarding glycogen and CP levels. Thus, the
biochemical changes during immediate and long-term adaptation to systematic muscle activity are reversible, with
the process o f direct and reverse development o f these changes being heterochronic.

      During overtraining, the chemistry o f the muscles and, above all, the oxidative processes are disturbed. Here
the glycogenolytic activity o f the muscle tissue diminishes, and levels o f ascorbic acid, glutathione, and glycogen
in it decrease (Platonov, 1988). Dysproteinaemia o f the blood plasma is noted, and the blood levels of
glycoproteins, sialic acids, and urea increase. With prolonged chronic fatigue, athletes have reduced functional
potential o f the sympathico-adrenal system, which is closely linked to a disruption o f the acid-base balance.

13:- **Reference material, not Eric's position**: `intencurriculumn.md` is Jason Avedesian's (Clemson) authored curriculum end to end, used by the Development Plan as a benchmark, not as something Eric wrote or necessarily agrees with. The two Unit Goal Programming Standards documents are explicitly staff templates filled in (thinly) by Geyer and Skodinski, not Eric. The AP Assessment Manual V12 and the TechnologyTemplateSOP (TMG) have uncertain/likely-legacy authorship (see Tensions below) and are marked accordingly.
35:- Applied Performance operates inside the Baylor Athletics Health & Wellness department, alongside (not above or below) Athletics Performance, Athletic Medicine, Performance Nutrition, and Mental Health Services. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md pp.5-6]
39:- A three-phase roadmap (Foundation, weeks 1-4; Operational Depth, weeks 5-10; Education and Culture, weeks 11-16+) is the stated plan to close those gaps, ending with an annual Playbook review cycle each May. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 4]
51:- Velocity-based 1RM estimation (linear-displacement transducer, ~10% load increments to 85-90% or a target mean velocity) is preferred over live 1RM attempts to avoid the fatigue and injury risk of true maxing, with published target mean velocities at 1RM (squat 0.3 m/s, bench 0.2 m/s, power hang snatch 1.0 m/s, power hang clean 0.8 m/s). **Inferred (author uncertain — legacy protocol, see Tensions)** [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md]
53:- The current data dictionary is organized by vendor (Catapult, Perch, ForceDecks, Polar), not by sport, which Eric's own gap analysis flags as a real usability problem for staff and a priority to fix with sport-specific, threshold-contextualized dictionaries. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3, Phase 2]
58:- Modified reactive strength index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker in place of subjective wellness questionnaires, because it is "objective, consistent, and actionable in a way the wellness surveys never quite were." **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]
99:- The traits easiest to build (aerobic) are lost fastest under detraining; the traits hardest to build (alactic/speed) are lost slowest — this ordering is used to sequence what needs the most frequent re-exposure. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md p.47]
108:- Applied Performance's stated role in return-to-performance is to supply information that supports Athletics Performance and Athletic Medicine's decisions on training and RTP periodization — a support/advisory role, not a stated final-decision role. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6]
155:- The full technology stack: Catapult (GPS), Kitman Labs (central AMS/data store), Perch (camera-based velocity-based training), Polar (heart rate), and the VALD suite — DynaMo, ForceDecks, ForceFrame, Hub, NordBord, SmartSpeed. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.7]
160:- Tensiomyography (TMG) is part of the toolkit, with a documented setup/operations SOP, but that SOP is headed with the names of a prior Director and Associate Director of Applied Performance (Althoff, Nelson), not Eric, and current active use is unclear from this corpus. **Inferred (legacy document, status unclear)** [technologytemplatesop.md]
165:- A standalone, 16-week Intern Sport Science Curriculum is proposed, deliberately separate from the Playbook so it can be distributed and revised on its own cycle, aligned to the NSCA Essentials of Sport Science (CPSS) textbook, and adapted from a Clemson model to Baylor's own technology stack (ForceDecks, Catapult, ForceFrame, NordBord, DynaMo, Perch, SmartSpeed, Polar) and to include football alongside Olympic-sport examples. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 5]
181:2. **Department reporting model is not internally consistent.** The Playbook (p.6) frames Applied Performance as a peer discipline inside Health & Wellness that "enables" Athletics Performance, Athletic Medicine, Nutrition, and Mental Health to answer their own questions. But Week 1 course material lists "Applied Performance" as one of many training sub-categories nested under Athletic Performance itself (p.11), and the same transcript narration describes Rash's role as "helping program and plan the training" — a support-staff framing, not a peer-department framing. Which model actually governs day-to-day authority is not reconciled anywhere in these documents.
183:3. **Coach's-eye-first versus objective-first is argued both ways.** The course material repeatedly argues that "you don't need a fancy test... you have to have a good coach's eye" and criticizes the GPS/load-monitoring era for breeding a fear-driven under-training culture. Eric's own SportSmith writing moves the opposite direction on daily monitoring specifically: he replaced subjective wellness surveys with objective force-plate mRSI because subjective self-report couldn't be trusted. Both share a skepticism of trendy or convenient data, but they land on opposite defaults (trust the trained eye vs. require an objective number) for the daily-monitoring question specifically.
185:4. **The Assessment Manual (V12) reads as an older document than the current technology stack.** It builds its 1RM-estimation protocol around GymAware, and its CMJ description references a "contact mat" for jump height. The current Playbook technology stack and the Development Plan both center velocity-based training on Perch, not GymAware, and the current Force Plate Testing V3 protocol runs all CMJ variants exclusively on ForceDecks force plates, with no contact mat mentioned. This suggests the Assessment Manual predates the current VALD/Perch-centered stack and may be a legacy document rather than the currently operative protocol — worth confirming directly with Eric before treating any of its specifics as current practice.

the muscle, and not the direct lengthening o f contracted muscic, is responsible for the storage o f elastic energy
within the SEC.

    Furthermore, it has been shown that mechanical strain imposed by stretching a contracted muscle is smaller in
amuscle with a preponderance o f ST (slow twitch) fibres, whereas the stored elastic energy is greater in FT fibres
(Komi, 1984). The same study has also suggested that the elasticity o f the SEC in a slow muscle is greater than
that in a fast muscle. These differences are largely due to the fact that the concentration o f collagen is higher in
slowmuscle than in fast muscle (Kovanen et al, 1984). Such findings agree with basic analysis o f slow and fast
 movements. The high stiffness and low strain o f a slow muscle clearly is most appropriate for muscle function
 which is intended for continuous support o f posture. Conversely, the lower stiffness, greater compliance and
 lower elasticity of a strongly contracting fast muscle is em inently suited to enhancing speed and efficiency o f
 movement. Further research has indicated that the differences in mechanical properties between fast and slow
 muscles in response to passive stretching are to a large extent due to their contcnt o f collagcn.

     In addition to the differences regarding the collagenous component of muscle, there are also differences in
 terms of the muscle fibres. Apparently ST fibres may be able to sustain cross-bridge attachm ents for longer
 penods than FT fibres. Therefore, prolonged muscle contraction would tend to be more easily maintained in slow
 postural (tonic) than in fast (phasic) musclcs. Consequently, stretching procedures would have to be applied for
 longer periods on slow muscles to significantly enhance their flexibility.

     The muscic fibres can also stretch passively and store elastic energy, like tendons. In this respect, the myosin
 cross-bridges that are considered to pull the actin filaments between the myosin filaments during muscle
 contraction, arc known to be compliant structures which may stretch considerably before they detach from the
 activated sites on the actin filaments. It is believed that this compliance may be caused by rotation o f the
 meromyosin heads of the cross-bridges and by elongation o f its tail, which appears to have a helical structure that
 would promote extensibility (Huxley, 1974). In other words, even a contracted muscle can stretch, not only due
 toitscollagenous component, but also due to its contractile tissue.

     As stated earlier, if a relaxed muscle is stretched beyond its resting length, it is the PEC which appears to be
 most exposed to the resulting tension, whereas in active muscle it is the SEC which is subjected to most tension.
 This implies that static, relaxed ballistic and passive stretching have the greatest effect on the PEC, while tense
 ballistic and active stretching affects predominantly the SEC. The various physiotherapeutic PNF (Proprioceptive
 Neuromuscular Facilitation) flexibility techniques appear to be able to stretch and strengthen both the SEC and

                                                                     41
                                                                  SUPERTRAINING

the PEC, as well as the associated muscles. Weight and other rcsistancc training routines based on the same PNF
principles can achieve similar results.
